Evidence informing this proposal [L04] [L05]

LiteLLM comparison · Original ID ADR-028 · Source record

C1 disposition. Historical product-specific proposal. No transfer of product behavior, license entitlement or acceptance to Aperture. Revalidate time-sensitive claims before a new procurement or deployment decision.
ADR-028Separate process health, readiness and graceful drainingProposed
Area Operations and resilienceSuggested owner Site reliability leadDate 6 October 2026

Context

A running process, reachable database and successful model request describe different kinds of health. Using one probe for all of them can cause restart storms or route traffic to an unusable service. Shutdown must also account for long-lived streams and pending asynchronous accounting work.

Options considered

  • One end-to-end probe for every lifecycle decision: rejected because provider or shared-state failure can unnecessarily restart healthy processes.
  • Separate liveness, readiness and synthetic service checks: selected, with outcomes aligned to the chosen dependency failure policy.
  • Immediate termination on rollout: rejected where it would cut streams and abandon accounting without a documented application recovery path.

Proposed decision

Use process liveness to identify a stuck runtime, readiness to express whether the instance should accept new work, and synthetic checks to observe the complete user path. Align load-balancer and DNS decisions with the selected fail policy. Drain new admissions before termination and bound the time allowed for active streams and queued work to finish.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • Failures can be diagnosed and contained more precisely, while probe design becomes part of the service contract rather than a copied deployment default.
  • Long-running requests can extend rollout or scale-in time; after the agreed drain deadline, clients and accounting must follow a declared incomplete-work procedure.

Required validation

  • Provider failure does not trigger an unnecessary process restart, while loss of required authorization state produces the intended readiness and routing result.
  • During rollout and scale-in, new work stops, existing streams finish or terminate as specified, and remaining queued work is accounted for visibly.

Revisit trigger

Review when dependency failure policy, ingress behavior or new long-lived protocols change what the service should admit during degradation and shutdown.

ADR-029Establish multi-zone availability before regional expansionProposed
Area Operations and resilienceSuggested owner Infrastructure resilience leadDate 6 October 2026

Context

A second region is not automatically the simplest answer to instance or zone failure. It introduces data, coordination and recovery choices beyond replica placement. The organization should first remove local single points of failure and establish measurable objectives before committing to a more complex regional topology.

Options considered

  • One instance and one zone: reject for the reference production service unless the business explicitly accepts the resulting outage exposure.
  • Multiple zones within one approved region: selected as the initial availability baseline with resilient state services.
  • Immediate multi-region deployment: defer until agreed recovery or locality requirements justify its added coordination, data and operating complexity.

Proposed decision

Spread serving capacity across failure zones and use appropriately resilient managed PostgreSQL and Redis configurations. Reserve capacity for a zone loss and align disruption controls with that design. Define business-approved availability, recovery-time and recovery-point objectives before regional expansion; treat these values as requirements to agree and test, not capabilities assumed from replica count.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • Common local failures can be handled with less complexity than a global topology, but a region-wide event still requires a deliberate recovery plan.
  • Resilience consumes standby capacity and operational attention; replicas do not protect against shared configuration mistakes, compromised credentials or unrecoverable encrypted state.

Required validation

  • A controlled zone-loss exercise maintains the accepted capacity and behavior while database and Redis failover complete within approved recovery objectives.
  • Loss of one serving replica, planned maintenance and disruption-budget behavior do not combine to remove all healthy capacity from service.

Revisit trigger

Reopen when region outage exposure, user geography or contractual recovery requirements exceed what the qualified single-region design can provide with acceptable risk.

ADR-030Allocate quotas by regional enforcement domainProposed
Area Operations and resilienceSuggested owner Global platform and FinOps architectDate 6 October 2026

Context

Geographically distributed gateways can share durable records while making admission decisions through separate regional coordination stores. That arrangement favors latency but does not automatically provide one atomic global quota. The organization must define whether limits apply per region, globally or through explicit allocations.

Options considered

  • Regional limits presented as global: rejected because simultaneous regional traffic could exceed the expectation communicated to application owners.
  • Regional quota allocations with reconciliation: selected when regional latency and isolation matter more than a fungible global pool.
  • One global coordination domain: consider for strict global admission, accepting cross-region latency and a larger common dependency.

Proposed decision

Before enabling additional regions, partition capacity and spending allowances into explicit regional allocations whose sum respects the approved global envelope. Document redistribution and failover rules and reconcile global usage separately. If strict globally shared admission is mandatory, qualify a common coordinator and its partition behavior instead of relying on a shared database alone.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • Applications receive honest regional and global limit semantics, but unused allocation may remain stranded until an authorized rebalance occurs.
  • Failover can create sudden demand in the surviving region; capacity and budget must be reserved or transferred deliberately without briefly granting both regions the same allowance.

Required validation

  • Simultaneous regional load and network partitions remain within the declared combined exposure, with no hidden multiplication of quota after failover.
  • An allocation transfer has a traceable owner and does not authorize overlapping excess capacity; global reconciliation identifies delayed or missing regional usage.

Revisit trigger

Review when regional traffic imbalance, latency goals or contractual spending rules justify changing from allocated limits to a shared global admission service.

ADR-031Recover configuration, durable state and encryption material togetherProposed
Area Operations and resilienceSuggested owner Disaster recovery ownerDate 6 October 2026

Context

Container recovery is insufficient when keys, policy, usage or provider credentials remain unavailable. Database state, encryption material and configuration must be compatible. Restoring older state can also reintroduce revoked access or stale counters, requiring security and accounting reconciliation.

Options considered

  • Database backups alone: rejected because restored encrypted credentials and effective configuration may remain unusable or inconsistent.
  • Coordinated recovery set: selected with versioned configuration, authorized encryption material, database recovery and post-restore reconciliation.
  • Live replica as the only recovery mechanism: rejected because it can reproduce corruption, mistaken policy changes or malicious mutations.

Proposed decision

Maintain a recovery manifest linking database recovery points, application versions, configuration revisions and authorized secret recovery. Rehearse restoration into isolation, including credential decryption and access reconciliation. Rebuild disposable payload caches rather than treating them as authoritative. Define handling for buffered spend, revoked identities and provider resources created after the restored point.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • Recovery can be measured as a complete service outcome, but protected access to backup encryption material and historical configuration requires deliberate governance.
  • Restoration may temporarily disagree with external provider activity or recent administrative changes; the service should not resume until accepted reconciliation and access checks are complete.

Required validation

  • An isolated restore authenticates approved workloads, denies known revoked access and successfully uses stored credentials without depending on unrecovered live infrastructure.
  • Timed recovery records achieved RTO/RPO, missing or replayed spend and external resource discrepancies, with explicit approval before recovered traffic is accepted.

Revisit trigger

Repeat after material schema, encryption, identity or topology changes and whenever a recovery exercise reveals an assumption absent from the manifest.

ADR-032Verify artifact provenance and maintain an active patch processProposed
Area Operations and resilienceSuggested owner Software supply-chain security leadDate 6 October 2026

Context

A gateway holds valuable credentials while providers and software evolve rapidly. Package names and mutable tags do not establish reproducible content. Artifact approval must work alongside vulnerability response because neither indefinite version freezing nor automatic upgrading provides sufficient assurance.

Options considered

  • Automatically deploy the newest package or rolling tag: rejected because origin, content and behavioral changes are not reviewed before production.
  • Verified immutable artifacts with staged promotion: selected, alongside advisory monitoring and an assigned emergency patch owner.
  • Long upgrade delays as the primary defense: rejected because delay neither proves artifact safety nor preserves security support indefinitely.

Proposed decision

Pin approved image digests and verify signatures against an independently controlled trust root before promotion. Record dependency and advisory assessment with each release. Track the supplier's current supported-version window and apply urgent fixes through an expedited version of the same pipeline. Revalidate signing-key changes and never interpret a valid signature as proof of secure code.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • Deployments become reproducible and their origin reviewable, while the platform must continuously fund compatibility qualification, advisory triage and trust-root maintenance.
  • Provenance controls reduce certain supply-chain risks but cannot eliminate a compromised trusted build or application vulnerability; runtime isolation and incident response remain necessary.

Required validation

  • Unsigned, unexpected-digest and unapproved artifacts fail the deployment gate, while the approved image is traceable to its release and review evidence.
  • An advisory simulation identifies affected deployments, produces a qualified replacement and exercises rollback or forward recovery within the organization's response objective.

Revisit trigger

Reopen after a supplier incident, signing or publishing change, altered support policy or evidence that patch response no longer meets organizational risk requirements.

C1 disposition. Historical product-specific proposal. No transfer of product behavior, license entitlement or acceptance to Aperture. Revalidate time-sensitive claims before a new procurement or deployment decision.
ADR-033Control callbacks and extensions as privileged codeProposed
Area Operations and resilienceSuggested owner Gateway application security leadDate 6 October 2026

Context

Custom hooks inspect requests, modify responses and access runtime context. They introduce dependencies, destinations and failure modes outside the standard contract. Extensions should therefore be treated as privileged application code in a credential-bearing service, with explicit ownership and review.

Options considered

  • Unreviewed in-process extensions: rejected because they inherit powerful access and can alter every participating application's behavior.
  • Reviewed, versioned minimal callbacks: selected only where documented configuration cannot meet the required behavior.
  • External narrow policy services: prefer when isolation is worth the network dependency, with explicit timeout and failure contracts.

Proposed decision

Prefer documented configuration over custom execution. For necessary callbacks, assign an owner, review dependencies and data access, pin code with the release manifest and bound execution time. Restrict outbound destinations and secrets. Use an isolated external service for high-risk logic when feasible, and prohibit request-controlled imports, code or arbitrary command selection.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • Extensions remain possible without becoming an uncontrolled platform surface, but custom requirements now carry ongoing testing and support obligations.
  • Externalizing logic can improve privilege separation while introducing latency and availability dependencies; in-process code cannot be presumed sandboxed merely because it uses a plugin interface.

Required validation

  • A failing or hanging callback produces the selected timeout, rejection or telemetry behavior without unbounded resources or unauthorized payload export.
  • The release inventory identifies every extension and dependency, and synthetic request fields cannot select executable code or expand its permitted destinations.

Revisit trigger

Review when an extension's scope grows, its owner changes, a standard capability replaces it or an incident exposes unacceptable in-process privileges.

ADR-034Default-deny MCP access and isolate tool executionProposed
Area Agents and applicationsSuggested owner Agent platform security leadDate 6 October 2026

Context

Tool gateways can access external systems and perform actions, creating trust relationships beyond text generation. Permissions, upstream credentials and tool descriptions all matter. Empty-list and inheritance behavior must be understood before model credentials gain discovery or execution authority.

Options considered

  • Enable every configured MCP server for all keys: rejected because ordinary model access should not imply unrelated tool authority.
  • Explicit server/tool grants in an isolated execution boundary: selected, with application authorization for consequential actions.
  • Run arbitrary stdio tools inside the main gateway: rejected initially because executable dependencies would share a valuable credential-bearing runtime.

Proposed decision

Disable unused MCP routes and leave stdio execution off in the main gateway. When tools are required, grant explicit server and tool entitlements, use clear deny-all semantics and isolate execution and credentials. Constrain arguments, review or pin tool catalogs where supported, and apply default-on input/result policy without relying on inherited parent-request guardrail selection.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • Model access and tool authority remain separate, but onboarding tools requires permission design, upstream credential ownership and a larger application acceptance matrix.
  • Gateway checks cannot undo a completed external action or replace the target system's resource authorization; consequential actions still need appropriate application approval and recovery.

Required validation

  • A model-only key discovers and executes zero tools, while an approved tool identity can use only its listed servers, operations and argument scope.
  • Changed catalogs, poisoned results, absent guards and disabled stdio calls follow the declared policy; HTTP-success tool-error envelopes are recorded as failures.

Revisit trigger

Reopen when introducing new tool categories, executable transports, external user delegation or actions with materially different side effects and recovery requirements.

ADR-035Preserve provider ownership for stateful API resourcesProposed
Area Agents and applicationsSuggested owner Stateful API integration leadDate 6 October 2026

Context

Files, jobs, conversations and prior-response identifiers represent provider-side state. Similar endpoint names do not make those resources interchangeable. Follow-up requests must preserve the resource's tenant and origin when they are retried, polled, continued, transferred between replicas or deleted.

Options considered

  • Route stateful follow-ups like ordinary stateless completions: rejected because another deployment may not own or understand the resource.
  • Explicit origin and tenant binding: selected for every retained identifier, with a defined lifecycle and failure outcome.
  • Application-managed provider state: acceptable where intentional, but document the reduced portability and prevent unvalidated identifiers from crossing tenants.

Proposed decision

Track or reliably encode the tenant, provider, deployment and relevant region associated with stateful resources. Route continuation, polling and deletion to a compatible owner. Disable generic fallback where ownership cannot be preserved. Define retention, expiration, recovery and orphan cleanup, and document which workflows require application mediation rather than transparent gateway substitution.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • Stateful operations become predictable and isolated, but their portability is narrower than the portability of simple text generation.
  • Resource ownership information may need durable retention, and provider outages can make continuation unavailable even while another provider can serve new stateless requests.

Required validation

  • Create, poll, continue and delete representative resources across replicas; each operation reaches the correct provider and rejects another tenant's identifier.
  • Provider failover and gateway restoration produce a documented result for existing resources, with no accidental new resource or silent loss of ownership.

Revisit trigger

Review when adding another stateful endpoint, changing identifier translation or adopting a provider-independent application store for conversations and job lifecycle.

ADR-036Govern batch and media work with distinct admission rulesProposed
Area Agents and applicationsSuggested owner Asynchronous workload platform leadDate 6 October 2026

Context

Batch and media work can differ substantially from chat in cost, duration and payload size. A small submission may authorize a much larger workload. Admission must therefore understand total exposure rather than reuse token estimates that cannot represent the operation.

Options considered

  • Apply the chat budget policy unchanged: rejected where the gateway cannot estimate the complete asynchronous or media workload at admission.
  • Separate batch/media admission: selected with workload estimates, payload constraints, concurrency and completion reconciliation.
  • Disable these endpoints permanently: reject as a blanket rule, but keep them outside the initial contract until a required use case is qualified.

Proposed decision

Create separate service classes for batch and media operations. Require a bounded workload declaration or application-side estimate, constrain file and output sizes, and limit outstanding jobs and submission rate. Define cancellation and eventual-cost behavior. Admit only approved provider operations and reconcile final usage when completion evidence arrives, making uncertain estimates visible.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • Large delayed workloads cannot silently inherit chat's assumptions, while applications may need a submission workflow and an asynchronous status experience.
  • Some costs remain uncertain until completion or provider billing; cancellation may limit future work without reversing work already performed or charges already incurred.

Required validation

  • An oversized or underestimated batch/media request is rejected or escalated before accepted exposure exceeds its approved service-class envelope.
  • Delayed completion, failed jobs, cancellation and duplicate polling produce consistent resource ownership and accounting without repeatedly charging the submission estimate.

Revisit trigger

Reopen when a provider changes pricing or cancellation semantics, a new modality enters scope or workload estimates consistently miss accepted exposure limits.

ADR-037Keep application quality and evaluation ownership with product teamsProposed
Area Agents and applicationsSuggested owner Application product and evaluation leadDate 6 October 2026

Context

Authenticated, correctly routed requests can still produce unusable answers. Quality depends on prompts, retrieval, task context and downstream handling beyond gateway control. Model abstraction should preserve clear product accountability rather than implicitly assigning answer quality to infrastructure operators.

Options considered

  • Treat HTTP success and provider compatibility as quality acceptance: rejected because they do not measure whether the application achieved its task.
  • Application-owned evaluation with shared platform tooling: selected to connect model changes to user outcomes and risk.
  • Central platform approves every application's answers: reject as the sole model because domain expertise and product accountability remain with application owners.

Proposed decision

Require each production application to own a representative evaluation corpus, acceptance criteria and regression review for its model aliases.   • Infrastructure and product responsibilities remain clear, but application teams must budget for evaluations and maintain representative data as user needs change.

Required validation

  • A proposed model or fallback change passes application-specific quality and structured-output checks, including the failure cases most consequential to that product.
  • Production monitoring can distinguish gateway success from application task failure and triggers a controlled rollback or review when quality regresses.

Review when the application's task, user population, retrieval data or risk level changes enough to make its evaluation corpus unrepresentative.

ADR-038Contract explicitly for required entitlements and supportProposed

Context

Adoption combines software capability, licensing and operating responsibility. Documentation may describe differently entitled or immature features. Installing the gateway does not establish that identity, governance and support requirements are covered; the chosen artifact and agreement must be assessed together.

Options considered

  • Enterprise subscription: select when required native controls and contracted support justify cost and reduce a measured operational burden.
  • Assume all documented features and support are included: rejected because entitlement and response commitments must be verified for the chosen agreement.

Proposed decision

Build a version-specific inventory of required controls, their edition, deployment constraints and contract terms. Consequences and tradeoffs

  • Procurement reflects the real operating model, but both technical and commercial assumptions need periodic review as usage and requirements evolve.

ADR-039Qualify performance and SLOs with realistic trafficProposed

Overhead depends on request shape, concurrency, providers and enabled controls. Isolated benchmarks cannot predict the complete enterprise path. With no supplied traffic profile or objectives, performance claims remain hypotheses until stakeholders agree a representative workload and measurable service requirements.

Options considered

  • Adopt vendor throughput numbers as production capacity: rejected because hardware, features, providers and request distributions may differ materially.

Proposed decision

Agree traffic classes and proposed SLOs with application owners, then benchmark the exact release, topology and enabled controls.   • Capacity planning and comparative evaluation become reproducible, while qualification requires representative test data, provider cost and controlled measurement effort.
  • Higher throughput is not automatically better if it weakens policy or increases dropped accounting; operational and correctness gates remain part of performance acceptance.

  • Repeated runs of the declared workload meet agreed latency, availability and resource targets with governance enabled, and include a reproducible direct-provider comparison.
  • Load beyond the accepted envelope produces controlled admission and recovery rather than unbounded queues, memory growth or unexplained loss of accounting and traces.

Start with explicitly tested inference families and versioned logical aliases. Document parameters, errors, streaming semantics, provider ownership and allowed fallback targets. C1 disposition. Historical product-specific proposal. No transfer of product behavior, license entitlement or acceptance to Aperture. Revalidate time-sensitive claims before a new procurement or deployment decision.
BIF-ADR-019Retain administrative audit independently from request diagnosticsProposed
Area Observability and assuranceSuggested owner Security operations ownerDate 6 October 2026

Context

Administrative changes can alter the gateway's trust boundary and must remain attributable after application logs expire. Signed events and object archives help preserve evidence, but retention and archival are independent mechanisms. The service needs proof of completeness and recoverability, not only signature verification.

Options considered

  • Selected: protected audit events with separate retention, export permissions and signing-key custody.
  • Rejected: relying exclusively on mutable request logs or dashboard visibility for administrative evidence.
  • Selected: independently retained archives with monitored lag and a deletion margin.

Proposed decision

Record sensitive administrative actions with actor, target, outcome and change reference. Configure signing and retain historical verification keys separately. Archive to protected object storage where required, monitor unarchived windows, and keep database retention longer than the verified archival delay. Restrict audit export and retention changes to designated roles.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • Independent audit aids incident reconstruction while creating additional sensitive identity metadata and key-management work.
  • HMAC validates integrity of retained records; missing or unrecorded events still require reconciliation and coverage checks.

Required validation

  • Sensitive changes generate complete attributable events and unauthorized users cannot alter retention or export protected records.
  • Archive interruption, replay and retention exercises preserve reconciled event counts and historical signature verification.

Revisit trigger

Revisit when retention obligations, archive architecture, signing scheme or administrative API coverage changes, and after any missing-event incident.

BIF-ADR-020Rehearse migration, restore and rollback as one recovery contractProposed
Area Observability and assuranceSuggested owner Database recovery leadDate 6 October 2026

Context

Startup migrations can outlive an image rollback, and encrypted backups depend on retained keys. Asynchronous usage may also leave a restored snapshot behind actual provider spend. Recovery must reconstruct an authorized, financially coherent service rather than merely start a container.

Options considered

  • Selected: consistent backups, protected encryption material and representative restore exercises before upgrades.
  • Rejected: assuming Helm rollback reverses schema or that successful database import proves application recovery.
  • Selected: forward repair or full restore when an older image cannot safely read the migrated schema.

Proposed decision

Retain image, effective configuration, schema history, encryption material and ledger checkpoints as one recovery set. Rehearse migration on restored data, serialize the initial upgrade bootstrap, and validate before expanding replicas. Define RTO and RPO explicitly, reconcile post-snapshot spend, and recheck authorization before restoring traffic.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • Recovery preparation increases release effort but reduces surprises during irreversible schema changes.
  • A restore can discard legitimate recent changes; operators need a documented reconciliation and communication procedure.

Required validation

  • An isolated restore validates keys, roles, providers, logs, decryptability and accurate remaining budget against the recovery record.
  • Interrupted migrations and attempted downgrades follow a documented safe path without silently losing records or reopening access.

Revisit trigger

Revisit whenever schemas, encryption, persistence backends or asynchronous accounting change, and when a restore drill misses its recovery objectives.

BIF-ADR-021Verify artifact provenance and patch against actual exposureProposed
Area Observability and assuranceSuggested owner Product security leadDate 6 October 2026

Context

Historical advisories describe particular versions and deployment prerequisites, while vendor security statements describe processes rather than the artifact an organization runs. Module versions, dynamic plugins and Enterprise bases can change exposure. Patch decisions need an accurate inventory and controlled evidence.

Options considered

  • Selected: digest-pinned artifacts, provenance review and an owned vulnerability-response process.
  • Rejected: declaring an image safe because a repository tag is newer or a vendor advertises scanning.
  • Selected: regression qualification tailored to management, URL-fetch and executable-extension attack surfaces.

Proposed decision

Inventory transport, core, framework, plugins, image and Enterprise base versions. Validate available provenance and scan the actual artifacts, track advisories and resolve ambiguous version ranges with the maintainer. Prioritize patches by reachable exposure, rehearse deployment and rollback, and preserve regression evidence for previously affected boundaries.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • Version precision improves response quality while adding review work and emergency patch obligations.
  • Some provenance or private-edition evidence may require vendor support; an unresolved gap remains an explicit acceptance exception.

Required validation

  • The inventory maps each official advisory to the deployed component and records why it is applicable, fixed or uncertain.
  • A patched candidate passes the relevant authorization and egress regressions before production promotion.

Revisit trigger

Revisit upon a new advisory, compromised build dependency, changed Enterprise base, unsupported release line or failure to obtain required artifact evidence.

BIF-ADR-022Treat native extensions as part of the trusted gatewayProposed
Area Extensions and lifecycleSuggested owner Extension review ownerDate 6 October 2026

Context

Native Go plugins share the gateway process and may influence identity, routing and per-attempt behavior. Their build compatibility and hook position affect correctness as well as security. An extension is therefore a release component with authority, not a harmless configuration addition.

Options considered

  • Selected: a small allowlist of reviewed native extensions built and pinned with the host.
  • Rejected: arbitrary runtime plugin URLs or unreviewed code loaded through administration.
  • Deferred: deprecated or planned extension mechanisms until a supported implementation satisfies the required contract.

Proposed decision

Approve each extension's hook placement, inputs, secret access, network effects, timeout and idempotency. Keep credential-supplying transport hooks distinct from post-authentication hooks and per-attempt LLM hooks. Build against the qualified host, disable unneeded loading paths, and require application authorization for every extension-induced external side effect.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • Custom behavior remains possible but expands the trusted codebase and couples release compatibility.
  • Panic recovery or type checking cannot contain arbitrary native code; strong isolation requires an external execution boundary.

Required validation

  • Hook-order tests show identity and mandatory policy cannot be weakened by extension placement or short-circuit responses.
  • Retry, reload, timeout and shutdown exercises demonstrate bounded execution and no duplicate unauthorized side effects.

Revisit trigger

Revisit when a plugin changes, host ABI or lifecycle changes, or a supported isolated extension interface becomes available with evidence of equivalent functionality.

BIF-ADR-023Isolate tool execution and govern MCP as delegated authorityProposed
Area Extensions and lifecycleSuggested owner Agent platform security leadDate 6 October 2026

Context

MCP transports add tool discovery, delegated credentials and potentially local process execution to the gateway's trust boundary. A permitted model call does not authorize every tool action. Output inspection also cannot reverse a completed external mutation.

Options considered

  • Selected: default-deny tool registration and scoped remote executors with independent authorization.
  • Rejected: unrestricted stdio processes or broad tool credentials inside the shared inference gateway.
  • Deferred: autonomous multi-step execution until identity, approval and side-effect limits are demonstrated.

Proposed decision

Inventory approved servers and tools, require authenticated administration for changes, and isolate tool execution from gateway secrets. Bind each call to a principal and permitted action, validate arguments before execution, and enforce step, time and result-size limits. Configure explicit OAuth issuer and callback identities and preserve application-owned transaction approvals.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • Agent integration becomes reviewable while adding tool-specific policy, token and execution infrastructure.
  • Read-only tools still introduce data exposure; state-changing tools require idempotency and authorization at their actual target.

Required validation

  • Unapproved tools, unauthorized principals and malicious arguments cannot trigger external actions or access gateway secrets.
  • OAuth confusion, reconnect, timeout, repeated calls and partial agent failure preserve scoped identity and produce complete execution records.

Revisit trigger

Revisit when a tool gains new capabilities, authentication changes, local execution becomes necessary or agent autonomy expands beyond the approved action envelope.

BIF-ADR-024Keep service accountability, commercial terms and exit practicalProposed
Area Extensions and lifecycleSuggested owner Architecture review boardDate 6 October 2026

Context

An enterprise gateway is a long-lived organizational dependency. Open-source rights, Enterprise entitlements, operational support and application quality have different owners. A useful decision record must preserve those responsibilities and provide a feasible exit without assuming that compatible APIs eliminate switching costs.

Options considered

  • Selected: named service ownership, explicit commercial requirements and a maintained exit inventory.
  • Rejected: transferring application evaluation or business authorization to the gateway vendor by implication.
  • Selected: conditional adoption with measurable acceptance gates, reviewed exceptions and scheduled decision renewal.

Proposed decision

Contract for the required edition, support, license behavior and recovery assistance. Keep application quality evaluations, prompts and business authorization with application owners. Export portable aliases, policy definitions and reconciled usage, inventory provider-bound resources, and rehearse an alternative path. Accept these ADRs only after evidence, owners and remaining exceptions are recorded.

Consequences and tradeoffs

  • The organization preserves negotiating and migration options while funding portability and evaluation work.
  • Stateful provider resources and custom extensions can remain costly to move despite a compatible inference API.

Required validation

  • An exit exercise routes the approved contract corpus through an alternative and accounts for retained resources and outstanding usage.
  • The adoption review records signed ownership, entitlement evidence, acceptance results and expiry dates for every exception.

Revisit trigger

Revisit at contract renewal, major architectural change, material service failure or when an alternative meets the same contract with demonstrably better organizational outcomes.

Context

Shared consumer credentials obscure ownership and enlarge the impact of compromise. Model access, billing attribution and incident response need a verified workload identity. Generated keys and their one-time retrieval also need a secure provisioning workflow.

Options considered

  • Share one gateway key per department.
  • Issue separate credentials per workload and environment.
  • Require delegated end-user identity for every call.

Proposed decision

Assign a distinct consumer or approved identity mapping to each service/environment, with a named owner and scoped resource grants. Deliver secrets through the organization's secret channel, disable query-key use and prevent logging or unintended forwarding. Credential count increases, so automated provisioning and rotation are necessary. Attribution and containment improve. Applications must not reuse administrative tokens or embed provider credentials merely to avoid the lifecycle work.

Demonstrate provisioning, rotation, revocation, leak-free telemetry and correct attribution across replicas. Verify that one workload cannot use another's grants or management authority.

KG-ADR-012Assign one retry owner and a total deadlineProposed
AreaRouting and runtimeSuggested ownerApplication reliability leadDrafted6 October 2026

Context

SDK, gateway, ingress and application retries can multiply attempts and charges. A timeout after dispatch can leave work running. Repeating model generation, a provider-resource operation and a mutating tool action have different safety properties.

Options considered

  • Allow every layer's default retries.
  • Assign one owner per operation with an end-to-end deadline.
  • Disable all recovery at every layer.

Proposed decision

Define one retry owner for each operation family, bound attempts and elapsed time, and classify failures by dispatch and output state. Restrict fallback to the original eligible set. Stateful or side-effecting operations require owner-aware idempotency/reconciliation; do not replay after response content is released.

Consequences and tradeoffs

Some failures will be returned instead of hidden by retries, preserving correctness and cost visibility. Applications need explicit recovery for incomplete tasks. The platform gains a measurable bound on attempted work rather than a stack of independent timeout settings.

Required validation

Inject connection, provider, quota and timeout failures at several lifecycle points. Confirm the maximum attempts, total deadline, no cross-boundary fallback and correct uncertain-outcome classification.

Acceptance gates: KG-T05, KG-T06, KG-T17, KG-T18. Status: not executed.

Revisit trigger

A new SDK retry default, endpoint family, provider idempotency contract or latency objective.

KG-ADR-013Specify streaming and cancellation as first-class outcomesProposed

Context

Streaming commits status before the application result is complete. Tool arguments and usage can arrive incrementally, and output cannot be withdrawn once delivered. A disconnected client does not prove cancellation of provider computation or billing.

Options considered

  • Treat HTTP 200 as complete success.
  • Define terminal, partial, cancelled and uncertain outcomes.
  • Disable streaming for every workload.

Proposed decision

Publish the permitted stream events, termination rules, timeout phases and cancellation behavior. Prohibit transparent replay after output. Preserve partial/unknown usage for reconciliation and use buffered output where required preventive checks cannot coexist with incremental disclosure.

Consequences and tradeoffs

Client libraries and dashboards must understand incomplete responses. Some sensitive workloads lose interactive streaming benefits. The resulting contract prevents silent truncation and contradictory concatenated answers from being represented as success.

Required validation

Test every selected format through actual ingress with slow clients, malformed chunks, provider errors, tool fragments and disconnects before terminal usage. Confirm bounded buffers and accurate outcome metrics.

Context

A second geographic region adds identity, state, quota and data-governance complexity. Many initial failures can be addressed with multiple warm nodes across zones in one approved region. Merely drawing a standby does not provide provider or inspection capacity.

Options considered

  • Start with one unprotected node.
  • Establish a multi-zone service and prove its failure behavior.
  • Begin with active-active global routing.

Proposed decision

Build a multi-zone baseline in one approved processing region, with explicit node, provider and auxiliary capacity for the selected zone-loss scenario. Add regions only after a concrete recovery, latency or residency requirement justifies the additional design.

Consequences and tradeoffs

This limits initial complexity but does not cover complete regional loss. The residual regional risk must be accepted. Shared identity, Redis and inspection remain dependencies and need their own availability design.

Required validation

Lose a serving node and zone under representative traffic, verify limits and identity behavior, and demonstrate recovery without unsafe retries or policy gaps.

Acceptance gates: KG-T07, KG-T08, KG-T23. Status: not executed.

Revisit trigger

A regional continuity requirement, provider concentration risk or unacceptable measured recovery result.

Context

Regional failover can duplicate quota or spending authority when counters are not globally consistent. Cross-region movement can also violate model, document and retained-resource ownership. Global coordination trades simpler accounting for latency and availability dependence.

Options considered

  • Assume one configuration implies globally shared limits.
  • Allocate bounded regional authority with explicit rebalancing.
  • Use a separately qualified strongly coordinated global admission service.

Proposed decision

For the reference multi-region extension, allocate explicit provider capacity and spending envelopes to each region and reconcile centrally. Rebalance through an auditable authority transfer, not concurrent grants. Keep fallback inside the approved processing and resource-ownership envelope. Use a global service only when its latency and failure contract is accepted.

Consequences and tradeoffs

Unused capacity may remain stranded during a partition, reducing utilization but bounding risk. Operations need a reallocation procedure and regional observability. A failover cannot exceed the surviving region's approved authority merely because demand moved.

Required validation

Partition regions, activate recovery traffic and attempt simultaneous near-limit dispatch. Verify total authority, provider capacity and forbidden destination rejection.

KG-ADR-034Default-deny MCP tools and separate execution authorityProposed
AreaAgent and applicationSuggested ownerAgent security ownerDrafted6 October 2026

Context

MCP discovery, per-tool ACLs, aggregation and invocation credentials are distinct contracts. Per-tool rules can override defaults, and catalog visibility does not authorize an action on a business resource. An LLM's requested tool call must not become a grant of privilege.

Options considered

  • Publish all discovered tools under a shared powerful credential.
  • Use explicit catalog/tool grants and backend business authorization.
  • Expose only application-specific tool endpoints outside the gateway.

Proposed decision

Default-deny the published tool set and review every override. Authorize discovery and execution separately, use distinct discovery/invocation credentials, restrict forwarded headers and destinations, and require executor-side ownership checks and idempotency. Qualify delegated exchange only for the supported protocol/mode.

Consequences and tradeoffs

Tool onboarding requires security review and a negative-test corpus. Some catalog convenience is lost, but privilege is not inferred from model output, schema annotations or aggregator membership. Gateway and executor must share usable correlation without exposing secrets.

Required validation

Test missing/overriding ACLs, catalog caching, aggregation collisions, credential scope, argument manipulation, denied-call evidence and timeout after a mutating action.

Context

Foundry supplies model and application services, while APIM supplies a policy and API operating boundary. Adding a gateway can centralize useful controls but also adds latency, credentials, failure dependencies and duplicated mechanisms. Options considered

  • Direct native service calls with application-owned controls.
  • Established APIM managed gateway over approved Foundry endpoints.
  • Dedicated preview gateway, or a customer-operated alternative such as LiteLLM/Bifrost.

Proposed decision

Establish a bounded native Foundry contract first. Add an established APIM composition only for named shared requirements that cannot be met more simply at the application boundary. Evaluate the dedicated preview tier separately. Consequences and tradeoffs

The design preserves a direct behavioral baseline and prevents premature gateway commitment. It requires an explicit capability and responsibility inventory, and may leave simple applications on a separately governed direct path. An existing well-operated gateway is not replaced without evidence of benefit.

Required validation

Compare native and mediated fixtures, complete task quality, latency, operational effort and cost for representative callers. Test every allowed direct path for equivalent mandatory controls. Reject a composition with an unowned or bypassable invariant.

AZ-ADR-005Assign accountable identities to workloads and environmentsProposed
AreaIdentity and trustSuggested ownerIdentity platform ownerDrafted6 October 2026

Context

Shared credentials obscure ownership, make revocation disruptive and can give several teams the same apparent policy identity. APIM subscription keys, Foundry resource keys and Entra workload identities have different authority and lifecycle. Attribution metadata supplied by a caller cannot repair an untrustworthy credential model.

Options considered

  • Share one gateway/provider key across applications.
  • Issue separately controlled keys with documented limitations.
  • Prefer distinct Entra workload identities with explicit environment ownership.

Proposed decision

Use distinct workload identities for production services and environments where the selected endpoint supports them. Record owner, purpose, allowed APIs/models and credential lifecycle. Keep end-user identity separate and derive cost attribution from verified mappings. Permit keys only through an explicit exception inventory with narrow exposure, rotation and revocation tests; never use an administrator credential as a normal inference credential.

Consequences and tradeoffs

More identity objects and lifecycle automation are required. Incident containment and cost attribution become more precise. Key-only clients may need an application adapter or a bounded exception rather than an automatic broad grant.

Required validation

Demonstrate that one workload can be disabled without affecting unrelated applications. Verify owner attribution across aliases, caches, tools and asynchronous jobs and that client-supplied labels cannot charge another owner.

Acceptance gates: AZ-T02 · AZ-T03 · AZ-T11. Status: not executed.

Revisit trigger

A new application/environment, identity compromise, unsupported client authentication or organizational ownership change.

AZ-ADR-006Validate issuer, audience and runtime grants independentlyProposed
AreaIdentity and trustSuggested ownerSecurity/identity ownerDrafted6 October 2026

Context

A correctly signed token may belong to another tenant, another API or a principal without the required operation. Gateway runtime roles, Foundry project roles and backend service permissions must not be treated as interchangeable. The preview gateway now offers scoped Entra runtime grants, but older key descriptions remain relevant to key-mode risk.

Options considered

  • Accept any valid tenant token.
  • Check issuer/audience only and delegate all authorization to the backend.
  • Validate credential context and an explicit grant before resolving a backend.

Proposed decision

Require approved issuers and audiences plus applicable application roles or gateway asset grants. Bind caller context to verified claims. Keep backend token acquisition independent, with an explicit intended resource and destination. Qualify preview alias/MCP-server scope and role propagation; do not infer per-tool business permissions or narrow API-key grants from the new Entra surface.

Consequences and tradeoffs

Applications must request the correct token audience and receive deliberate grants. Misconfiguration fails earlier and more visibly. The policy owner must manage role definitions and claim changes rather than relying on a generic bearer-token check.

Required validation

Exercise wrong tenant, audience, role, principal and resource scope; test expiry and grant removal. Confirm that an authorization rejection produces no upstream dispatch and that downstream tokens are never returned to the caller.

Acceptance gates: AZ-T02 · AZ-T03 · AZ-T04. Status: not executed.

Revisit trigger

Identity-provider configuration, role definition, client authentication flow or gateway release changes.

AZ-ADR-007Enforce tenant and object isolation beyond projects and workspacesProposed
AreaIdentity and trustSuggested ownerApplication security and data ownersDrafted6 October 2026

Context

Foundry projects and APIM workspaces are administrative constructs with specific runtime behavior. They do not automatically authorize business documents, tool actions or stateful IDs. Resource keys can bypass the granular Foundry RBAC model, and indexed permission projections can be stale.

Options considered

  • Use project/workspace names as the sole tenant boundary.
  • Add application-owned authorization and separate identities to shared infrastructure.
  • Separate resources, gateways, stores or subscriptions for stronger isolation.

Proposed decision

Make tenant and resource isolation an end-to-end invariant. Derive tenant identity server-side; authorize every retrieval, conversation/file/job operation and tool action against the owner. Select physical/resource separation when shared controls cannot meet the threat model. Construct Search permissions from trusted identity and track their freshness. Test keys, direct paths and global policy inheritance rather than assuming a project or workspace confines them.

Consequences and tradeoffs

Some applications need separate resources or explicit ownership stores, increasing cost and administration. Shared deployments remain possible where negative tests prove isolation. Revocation and deletion must include caches, citations and active agent workflows.

Required validation

Perform cross-tenant enumeration, guessed-ID, filter-injection and tool-object tests. Measure source-permission revocation to denial across retrieval and cached answers. Inspect effective shared identities and grant inheritance.

Acceptance gates: AZ-T03 · AZ-T13 · AZ-T15 · AZ-T17 · AZ-T19. Status: not executed.

Revisit trigger

External tenants, more sensitive data, new stateful APIs, workspace adoption or permission-ingestion changes.

AZ-ADR-008Separate administration from inference and policy useProposed
AreaIdentity and trustSuggested ownerPlatform security ownerDrafted6 October 2026

Context

An operator who changes routes or policies may control which destinations receive content and which credentials the gateway can exercise. Runtime callers should not acquire that authority. Portal convenience can blur provisioning, development and production operations.

Options considered

  • Allow application teams broad service administration.
  • Delegate narrow API administration under enforced central policy.
  • Use separate production management identities, approvals and network exposure.

Proposed decision

Restrict administrative grants independently of runtime invocation. Use controlled deployment identities, named operator access and narrowly delegated scopes. Treat policy/backend edits as privileged security changes, especially where managed identities are assigned. Keep administration off application-facing routes and require attributable emergency changes followed by reconciliation into reviewed source.

Consequences and tradeoffs

Self-service becomes structured rather than unrestricted. Emergency edits remain possible but must be time-bounded, audited and reconciled. Separate management access reduces accidental credential and policy exposure without proving complete runtime isolation by itself.

Required validation

Attempt management operations with runtime identities and policy edits with restricted developer identities. Inspect role assignments, effective credential use and audit exports. Confirm management APIs are not exposed through inference routing.

AZ-ADR-009Separate encryption lifecycle from access credentialsProposed
AreaIdentity and trustSuggested ownerSecurity and key-management ownerDrafted6 October 2026

Context

Managed identities reduce static secrets but external providers, tool connections, certificates and customer data stores still introduce credential and encryption dependencies. Rotation and restoration have different purposes: rotating access should not make durable data unreadable, and restoring keys should not restore obsolete access.

Options considered

  • Embed provider keys and encryption values in deployment configuration.
  • Use managed identities and approved secret references with distinct key lifecycles.
  • Require customer-managed keys for every service regardless of available benefit or support.

Proposed decision

Prefer workload identity where supported; use controlled secret references otherwise. Maintain separate lifecycle and ownership for provider credentials, signing/TLS material and encryption keys. Record service-specific customer-key support and exclusions rather than making a blanket encryption claim. Restore key references and data coherently while reapplying current revocations and least-privilege grants.

Consequences and tradeoffs

Key and secret inventories become part of deployment and recovery. Customer-managed encryption can add availability dependencies and does not control every service processing path. Some external providers remain key-based and need bounded exceptions.

Required validation

Rotate identities and secrets under load, inspect every log/trace sink, disable key versions in nonproduction and restore the approved state/key set. Verify that clients never receive backend tokens or secrets.

AZ-ADR-010Bind routing to approved processing and network envelopesProposed
AreaIdentity and trustSuggested ownerNetwork and privacy ownersDrafted6 October 2026

Context

Gateway location, private connectivity, model processing geography and storage location are distinct properties. Global or data-zone model deployment can reach a broader processing scope than the gateway region. Safety, embedding, telemetry and tool calls introduce additional destinations beyond inference.

Options considered

  • Infer residency from the gateway or account region.
  • Approve every reachable destination and processing/storage contract.
  • Forbid all cross-region services even when the workload permits them.

Proposed decision

Approve a complete data-flow envelope per alias and workload: client/gateway/backend paths, model processing scope, state storage, safety/embedding services, tools and telemetry. Enforce destination and region restrictions before primary or fallback dispatch. Configure inbound and outbound private networking independently where required, and treat managed identity as authentication rather than network bypass. Unknown processing terms block the dependent sensitive workload.

Consequences and tradeoffs

Some models, router candidates or gateway regions may be excluded despite technical availability. The design can still use wider processing scopes where policy explicitly permits them. Network and privacy owners must participate in model and tool changes.

Required validation

Verify DNS, routing, public-path denial and all auxiliary recipients. Trigger fallbacks and confirm destination eligibility. Review service-specific retention/processing evidence for the actual deployment, not a generic catalog description.

AZ-ADR-011Separate semantic model selection from endpoint load balancingProposed
AreaRouting and runtimeSuggested ownerModel platform and SRE ownersDrafted6 October 2026

Context

Foundry model router changes which model performs a task, while APIM pools select endpoints and apply transport resilience. Both can be enabled at once, creating hidden selection and retry interactions. Models that share an input schema are not necessarily equivalent in quality, context or tools.

Options considered

  • Enable adaptive selection and fallback independently at every layer.
  • Use fixed approved aliases and simple equivalent-target pools initially.
  • Adopt one constrained router policy after task-level evaluation.

Proposed decision

Start with fixed approved models or equivalent deployment pools. Introduce semantic routing as a separately reviewed product capability with one accountable candidate-policy owner. Distinguish router decisions from transport attempts in evidence. Every candidate and fallback must satisfy the same authorization, state, feature and processing envelope; do not let a successful fallback override those requirements.

Consequences and tradeoffs

The initial design may forgo automatic cost/quality optimization but is easier to explain and recover. Later routing experiments need representative quality and complete-cost data. A change in candidate set is an application-facing release even when the alias remains stable.

Required validation

Compare fixed and routed task outcomes, verify all possible destinations and observe nested attempts under failure. Test long-context, tool and structured-output cases where apparent schema compatibility is insufficient.

Acceptance gates: AZ-T05 · AZ-T06 · AZ-T18 · AZ-T21. Status: not executed.

Revisit trigger

AZ-ADR-012Assign one retry owner and preserve the total deadlineProposed
AreaRouting and runtimeSuggested ownerRuntime platform ownerDrafted6 October 2026

Context

Applications, SDKs, APIM policies, router services and providers can each perform recovery. Multiplying retries can increase cost, overload a failing provider and duplicate tool effects. A client timeout does not reveal whether upstream execution happened.

Options considered

  • Accept each layer’s default retries.
  • Disable all recovery and return every transient failure.
  • Assign a bounded recovery owner and explicit retryability contract.

Proposed decision

Assign one recovery owner per route and document any unavoidable inner behavior. Bound total attempts, backoff and elapsed deadline across all layers. Retry only an eligible request against approved targets, accounting for possible prior execution. Do not replay after client-visible output, durable submission or a business side effect without an explicit idempotency/reconciliation contract. Carry remaining deadline and attempt context through the call graph.

Consequences and tradeoffs

Some transient failures become visible instead of being hidden by repeated attempts. Provider expense and tail latency become more predictable. The application must distinguish confirmed pre-dispatch failure from uncertain execution and expose a useful recovery path to users.

Required validation

Inject each failure class and count upstream dispatches. Verify deadline exhaustion, Retry-After handling, no unauthorized fallback and no duplicate business action. Confirm SDK retry configuration instead of relying on defaults.

Revisit trigger

SDK, policy, router or provider behavior changes; a new stateful or side-effecting route is introduced.

AZ-ADR-013Publish streaming, cancellation and incomplete-outcome semanticsProposed
AreaRouting and runtimeSuggested ownerApplication and API runtime ownersDrafted6 October 2026

Context

Streaming commits response headers and content before final model usage and success are known. Gateways may buffer, add events or terminate after a policy finding. A disconnected client can leave billable work running, and a partial tool argument stream is not an executable complete instruction.

Options considered

  • Treat HTTP 200 and socket closure as success.
  • Buffer every response before delivery.
  • Publish explicit streaming modes and outcome states with tested cancellation.

Proposed decision

Define complete, refused, policy-blocked, incomplete, client-cancelled and uncertain-upstream outcomes. Qualify ingress/gateway/provider event behavior, including usage-only chunks. Choose buffering versus incremental delivery per risk and latency requirement. Never silently replay or merge a second answer after visible output. Propagate cancellation where supported and preserve unresolved usage/spend until the upstream result is known.

Consequences and tradeoffs

Clients need protocol-aware parsers and explicit recovery UX. Preventive output checks may increase first-token latency. Financial reporting cannot always settle immediately on disconnect, and some provider operations may remain noncancellable.

Required validation

Interrupt streams at each lifecycle stage and use slow consumers. Assert event ordering, partial tool handling, terminal errors, cancellation acknowledgement and accounting status. Inspect actual bytes, not only gateway metrics.

Acceptance gates: AZ-T07 · AZ-T08 · AZ-T11. Status: not executed.

Revisit trigger

New client library, stream protocol, content-check mode, preview usage event or long-running model behavior.

AZ-ADR-014Qualify required safety controls by route and release boundaryProposed
AreaRouting and runtimeSuggested ownerSafety and application security ownersDrafted6 October 2026

Context

Foundry filtering, APIM content checks and application validators are separate mechanisms. Their scope, data destinations and timing differ. Streaming checks can detect content after earlier fragments were released; a text check cannot authorize a transaction or guarantee safe retrieval.

Options considered

  • Assume default model filtering covers every organizational requirement.
  • Apply every available guardrail without ownership or latency analysis.
  • Specify required preventive/detective controls per route and test their execution.

Proposed decision

Name the required check, enforcement point, inspected fields, failure policy and processing location for each endpoint. Use a hold-before-release design where complete prevention is mandatory, otherwise explicitly approve incremental exposure. Fail closed on unavailable mandatory checks. Keep business authorization and transaction validation outside model-content classification, and review every new safety recipient as a data flow.

Consequences and tradeoffs

Some workloads accept greater latency or cannot use an unqualified streaming path. Duplicate filtering is avoided unless it addresses a distinct requirement. Operators can distinguish a model refusal, a policy block and a broken detector.

Required validation

Inject safe synthetic markers into all relevant fields and fail the checking service. Assert no prohibited byte or action escapes required prevention, including cache hits, native passthrough and tools. Measure latency and false-positive impact.

AZ-ADR-015Keep exact response reuse off until eligibility is provenProposed
AreaData and financeSuggested ownerApplication/data ownerDrafted6 October 2026

Context

A cached answer can contain personalized or permission-sensitive data and can outlive its model, prompt or source policy. Native prompt-prefix caching is a different optimization from returning a previous complete result. Cost savings alone do not justify reuse across authorization boundaries.

Options considered

  • Enable broad response caching to reduce provider calls.
  • Disable complete-response reuse initially.
  • Permit explicitly eligible exact reuse with scoped keys and invalidation.

Proposed decision

Keep complete-response caching disabled at initial rollout. Permit exact reuse only for approved read-only requests with a key binding trusted tenant/permission context, model and prompt contract, safety policy and all relevant inputs. Authenticate and authorize every hit. Exclude side-effecting operations and sensitive personalized results unless a specific safe contract is demonstrated. Set retention and invalidation obligations.

Consequences and tradeoffs

Initial provider consumption may be higher. Cache behavior becomes understandable and tenant-safe. Model/policy/source changes may require invalidation and can create miss bursts that must fit capacity and budget.

Required validation

Test cross-owner requests, changed permissions, policy/model updates, expiry, deletion and cache outage. Demonstrate that hits do not bypass current authorization or mandatory safety checks and that reported cache savings use honest accounting.

Revisit trigger

AZ-ADR-016Treat semantic caching as an evaluated application featureProposed
AreaData and financeSuggested ownerProduct and retrieval ownersDrafted6 October 2026

Context

Semantic similarity can identify related questions without preserving the correct answer, time context or permission scope. APIM semantic caching introduces an embedding path and a configured cache, with feature availability dependent on topology. A similarity threshold is not a security or correctness guarantee.

Options considered

  • Use semantic caching as a transparent gateway optimization.
  • Use exact reuse only.
  • Run a separately governed semantic-reuse experiment for eligible tasks.

Proposed decision

Approve semantic caching independently of exact caching. Define eligible tasks, a permission-bound namespace, model/prompt versions, cache lifetime and a measured false-match tolerance. Include embedding and cache destinations in the privacy inventory. Do not ignore security-relevant system instructions or permit cross-tenant reuse. Verify the chosen gateway supports the required external cache configuration before deployment.

Consequences and tradeoffs

Evaluation and invalidation work can outweigh savings for low-repetition tasks. Similarity tuning is application-specific. A cache rollout can improve latency while degrading answer accuracy, so quality and authorization remain release gates.

Required validation

Use adversarial near-neighbor prompts, conflicting facts, different roles/tenants and revoked documents. Compare task correctness and complete cost against exact/no-cache baselines. Test cache-miss overload and deletion propagation.

AZ-ADR-017Assign durable authority across managed and customer stateProposed
AreaData and financeSuggested ownerPlatform/data architectDrafted6 October 2026

Context

Unlike a customer-operated gateway with one selected database, the Azure composition has several managed control planes and separate application stores. Desired policy, model deployments, conversations, search permissions and financial events have different authorities and restore semantics. Treating the whole stack as stateless conceals these dependencies.

Options considered

  • Assume managed services eliminate state-ownership decisions.
  • Copy all state into one customer database.
  • Identify the authoritative system and recovery contract for each state class.

Proposed decision

Maintain an authority map: reviewed source for desired configuration; Azure services for deployed resource state; the business system for permissions; the application for user/resource ownership; selected service stores for durable responses/jobs; and an explicit ledger for financial events. Record replication, consistency, retention, deletion and export behavior. Do not claim customer control over undocumented managed-service internals.

Consequences and tradeoffs

Recovery and governance require a composed inventory rather than one database backup. Some state is reconstructed, some exported, and some remains service-bound. The map enables honest portability and explains where an outage or restoration can create stale authority.

Required validation

Trace create/update/delete operations to their authority and replicas. Restore representative state classes, verify current permission and financial state, and demonstrate that inferred caches cannot become authoritative accidentally.

AZ-ADR-018Define coordination by actual gateway enforcement domainProposed
AreaData and financeSuggested ownerPlatform/SRE ownerDrafted6 October 2026

Context

APIM operational counters and backend circuit decisions do not form one globally serialized gateway state. Regional and workspace gateways can enforce independently. A Redis deployment from another product’s reference architecture does not automatically become APIM’s coordination mechanism.

Options considered

  • Repeat one organization-wide limit on every gateway and call it global.
  • Allocate limits per actual gateway/region and measure aggregate exposure.
  • Use an external authority for invariants requiring stronger coordination.

Proposed decision

Inventory where each token, request, concurrency and circuit state is evaluated and shared. Define trusted counter keys and avoid inconsistent settings for reused keys. Allocate operational allowances by enforcement domain; use a separately qualified authority when global consistency is required. Keep optional payload caches distinct from rate, authorization and financial state.

Consequences and tradeoffs

Regional allowances can strand capacity and require controlled rebalancing. Counter behavior remains useful for traffic governance without being misrepresented as global financial correctness. Additional coordination is justified only by a stated invariant.

Required validation

Run synchronized bursts through every selected gateway and partition. Observe combined admission, counter reset and recovery, including streams and cached results. Record overshoot and allocate headroom based on evidence rather than zero-overshoot assumptions.

AZ-ADR-019Separate strict spending authorization from operational budgetsProposed
AreaData and financeSuggested ownerFinOps and platform ownersDrafted6 October 2026

Context

Token controls, observed cost policies and invoice totals are different mechanisms. Streaming estimates, concurrent calls, tool charges and asynchronous jobs make an unconditional hard-cap claim unsafe without a bounded dispatch model. The preview tier’s cost-limit scope does not by itself establish that model.

Options considered

  • Accept soft budgets with documented exposure and alerts.
  • Treat a token/cost counter as an exact financial ceiling.
  • Implement a bounded reservation authority for selected strict workloads.

Proposed decision

Classify each workload as soft-budget or strict-admission. For strict workloads, require a conservative cost bound, serialized reservation or non-overlapping regional allocation, one-use dispatch permission and durable settlement. Fail closed when authority or pricing cannot establish the bound. Retain uncertain execution exposure. Exclude or explicitly constrain unbounded agent/tool/job costs rather than silently weakening the guarantee.

Consequences and tradeoffs

Strict admission adds availability and engineering dependencies and can reject work conservatively. Soft-budget workloads remain simpler but must carry a named exposure acceptance. Unresolved reservations can reduce usable capacity until reconciliation.

Required validation

Race near-limit calls, remove prices, fail the ledger, crash around dispatch and settle duplicate/late events. Demonstrate the claimed maximum exposure for each supported contract; classify unsupported cases honestly.

AZ-ADR-020Reconcile usage with an attributable attempt ledgerProposed
AreaData and financeSuggested ownerFinOps/data ownerDrafted6 October 2026

Context

A user call can include multiple provider attempts, cached outcomes, safety/embedding calls and tool actions. Sampled telemetry and final response usage may omit failed or incomplete work. Provider bills can use dimensions and timing that differ from application traces.

Options considered

  • Use sampled observability dashboards for chargeback.
  • Persist only successful final response usage.
  • Maintain durable attributed events and reconcile them against billing evidence.

Proposed decision

Record call, attempt, job and tool identities with owner, alias/model, policy version, reported/estimated usage, price basis and uncertainty. Make settlement idempotent and correction-aware. Reconcile aggregates against actual available billing/export dimensions; do not invent a per-request join where unsupported. Keep unknown amounts visible and assign exception owners. Retain operational metrics separately from financial authority.

Consequences and tradeoffs

Storage, reconciliation and privacy work increase. Chargeback becomes explainable and failures are no longer falsely free. A complete account can lag the user response when jobs or uncertain attempts settle later.

Required validation

Compare synthetic dispatch counts with event and settlement totals, replay events, lose final stream trailers and reconcile a selected billing period. Investigate every unattributed attempt or unexplained variance before approving chargeback.

Store security-sensitive configuration and model contracts in versioned source. Assign explicit ownership to generated, delegated and runtime-managed objects. Proposed decision

Start with the minimum composed service that satisfies the approved contract. Isolate high-risk tool execution, sensitive tenant boundaries and strict financial authority when required. Context

Options considered

  • Size by average requests per second alone.
  • Overprovision every dependency without workload evidence.
  • Model the complete concurrency and token distribution and test saturation.

Proposed decision

Use representative input/output distributions, active durations and policy paths to size gateways, model deployments and dependencies. Bound concurrent work and queues before relying on autoscaling. Keep retry and regional allocation effects in the model. Qualify provisioned-throughput economics and actual deployment capacity against the workload rather than treating quota as a performance commitment.

Consequences and tradeoffs

Capacity planning needs realistic traces or synthetic distributions and periodic refresh. Conservative admission may reject bursts, while unconstrained scaling is avoided. Optimizations such as caches or router choices require rerunning the sizing model when their hit rates or output profiles change.

Required validation

Load test matched native and gateway paths through saturation, including slow consumers, long outputs, cold caches and failed dependencies. Measure latency percentiles, active connections, token admission and recovery rather than a single peak throughput number.

Bind every stateful resource to a verified owner, originating service/deployment, policy and retention contract. Authorize read, continue, list, cancel and delete independently. Route only to compatible origin services; any reconstruction or migration is explicit and privacy-reviewed. Preserve current authorization on session continuation and include derived artifacts and logs in deletion inventory.

Consequences and tradeoffs

The application needs an ownership mapping and cannot promise transparent cross-provider state portability. Some failover scenarios require a new session or controlled reconstruction. Resource cleanup becomes an auditable lifecycle rather than a best-effort client request.

Required validation

Use guessed/leaked IDs across users, replay IDs after revocation and attempt continuation through another deployment. Test deletion, restore and session migration without restoring unauthorized access.

AZ-ADR-036Govern batch, background and media work separatelyProposed
AreaAgent and applicationSuggested ownerApplication and FinOps ownersDrafted6 October 2026

Context

Asynchronous and media workloads have different payload sizes, completion times, retention and cost units from ordinary chat. Submission acceptance can precede billable execution by a long interval. A client timeout can create ambiguity about whether a durable job was created.

Options considered

  • Apply the ordinary chat timeout, limits and accounting unchanged.
  • Block all noninteractive workloads.
  • Create distinct admission, ownership and settlement contracts for each family.

Proposed decision

Qualify batch, background Responses and media endpoints independently. Bound input/output exposure, retain owner and origin, persist submission intent and provider IDs, and use supported idempotency or reconciliation for ambiguous outcomes. Authorize polling, output access, cancellation and deletion. Set explicit retention and delayed-settlement rules; do not release all exposure merely because the submitter disconnected.

Consequences and tradeoffs

Long-running workloads require durable coordination and cleanup. Some jobs cannot support an immediate hard cancellation or precise upfront cost; those limitations must be accepted or excluded. The gateway can mediate submission without becoming the authoritative job scheduler.

Required validation

Test oversized submissions, duplicate attempts, partial completion, expired credentials, delayed usage, cancellation limits and restart recovery. Confirm no cross-owner output access and no hidden provider jobs after an ambiguous request.

Context

Define product SLOs and an incremental gateway-overhead budget before tests.   • Use a fixed target without fallback.
  • Use reviewed candidates with explicit eligibility and failure rules.

Start with a small fixed or weighted approved candidate set. Evaluate eligibility before every attempt using verified caller scope, contract capabilities, state ownership, location and remaining admission authority.   • Disable all recovery attempts.
  • Assign one upstream retry owner with classification, attempt and deadline budgets.

Context
