Context

Operational token counters and financial alerts do not establish an unconditional dispatch-time spending limit. Concurrent requests, late usage and unknown execution can create exposure beyond a nominal allowance. A stricter service must state its assumptions.

  • Qualify native preview spend cap budgets as a secondary project/service containment control.
  • Reject all uncertain-cost workloads.

Classify budgets as approximate operational guidance or strict admission policy. For strict classes, atomically reserve conservative maximum exposure before dispatch using trusted tenant, price version and bounded work. Unknown estimation fails closed or consumes a separately approved fixed allowance. Record each authorized attempt, retain uncertain exposure after dispatch and allocate bounded regional authority. Never describe this customer component as an Apigee built-in guarantee or an absolute invoice ceiling outside its workload assumptions. Evaluate the native preview spend cap first; use it where its documented scope and delayed enforcement are acceptable, alongside rather than as proof of a stronger tenant-level reservation guarantee.

Stricter controls can reject useful work and temporarily hold unused funds. They add a critical dependency and reconciliation workload. Approximate workloads can use simpler controls when their owners explicitly accept overshoot and evidence limits.

Required validation

Race calls at the allowance edge; inject duplicate dispatch, missing price, crash, timeout and partition. Verify reservation invariants and declared residual exposure, then compare observed settlement and billing aggregates. Where a native cap is selected, test its enforcement and restoration workflow, owner permissions, residual charges and rearming behavior without affecting unrelated production services.

Context

  • Collect all available logs without a coverage plan.

Define an audit matrix for policy publication, shared-flow change, role binding, product/app grant, key revocation, backend identity, catalog change and sensitive resource operations. Explicit auditing increases storage and operational work, and some categories need additional configuration. It improves incident reconstruction while discouraging unnecessary prompt retention. Missing required evidence becomes a visible acceptance failure.

Before upgrade, record runtime/platform, Cassandra arrangement, backup format, customer schema and key compatibility. Rehearse the supported target upgrade and recovery path in isolation. Context

A process can answer a health endpoint while using stale configuration, lacking credentials or failing an essential safety/counter dependency. Conversely, a remote telemetry outage may not justify removing healthy serving capacity.

  • Make readiness require every optional service.
  • Define layered health and dependency-specific readiness/draining.

Proposed decision

Distinguish process liveness, runtime readiness, effective policy freshness, credential availability, model-path health and optional integration health. Readiness gates only dependencies required by the admitted workload class. Bound stale operation and publish its status. Before planned removal, stop new admission, drain eligible in-flight work, record incomplete/cancelled outcomes and reconcile outstanding reservations. Consequences and tradeoffs

The health model is more complex but prevents both false availability and unnecessary cascading outages. Draining long streams may require an explicit maximum wait and controlled interruption policy.

Context

A global budget or quota label does not guarantee a global atomic balance. If every disconnected region independently admits against the full allowance, business exposure can multiply precisely during an outage.

  • Let each region consume the full global limit.
  • Require one always-online global authority for every call.
  • Allocate bounded regional authority with explicit reconciliation and rebalancing.

Proposed decision

For strict-budget workloads, assign bounded regional spending authority before isolated operation. Preserve reservation and attempt ownership locally under a durable supported mechanism. Rebalance only through an authenticated, audited transfer that prevents double allocation. During partition, exhaust only the assigned share; do not fall back to unlimited local counters. Approximate rate limits can use looser semantics only under a separately approved overshoot contract.

Consequences and tradeoffs

Unused allowance in a healthy region may not immediately rescue another region, reducing availability compared with unrestricted admission. The tradeoff makes financial exposure bounded and explainable during the most uncertain period.

Required validation

Partition regions while near limits, replay transfers, restore stale state and reconcile concurrent attempts. Demonstrate conservation of authority and the declared maximum residual exposure after recovery.

Context

AreaArchitecture & trustSuggested ownerPlatform architectDrafted7 October 2026

Context

The reference organization needs accountable model access across teams but has not demonstrated that one additional gateway is necessary for every application. Commercial administration can replace engineering work while introducing a vendor dependency and another privileged execution layer. The choice must be based on the complete operating service.

Options considered

  • Retain direct provider access with application controls.
  • Adopt Portkey/SCM as the shared commercial gateway.
  • Retain an incumbent gateway or compose narrowly separated services.

Proposed decision

Establish a native or incumbent control group, then qualify Portkey for the requirements it demonstrably improves: shared provider access, governed configuration, administration or security integration. Start with a bounded LLM contract and an accountable service owner. Keep task authorization, quality and any strict monetary service explicitly assigned. Do not make adoption of MCP, agents, prompt hosting or additional security products implicit in the gateway decision.

Consequences and tradeoffs

This can preserve more than one approved integration pattern and requires a clear rule for when shared mediation is mandatory. It avoids paying for duplicated controls and makes the commercial benefit measurable, but adds upfront comparison work.

Required validation

Run the same capability, policy, failure and cost fixtures through both paths. Demonstrate the additional controls and attempted bypasses. Approval requires a documented requirement and benefit, not a broad feature score.

Acceptance gates: PK-T01, PK-T02, PK-T03, PK-T24. Status: not executed.

Revisit trigger

Provider scope, team count, operating capacity or a mandatory governance requirement changes.

PK-ADR-002Qualify OSS, Enterprise, SCM and special modes separatelyProposed
AreaArchitecture & trustSuggested ownerPlatform security architectDrafted7 October 2026

Context

Public source visibility, a commercial runtime and a managed administration experience are different evidence boundaries. A shared name or ancestry cannot prove matching controls. The retrieved release channels also use different version numbers and may not represent the current tenant rollout.

Options considered

  • Treat all Portkey-branded distributions as equivalent.
  • Standardize on one exact qualified distribution and release set.
  • Support several distributions with separate capability and assurance records.

Proposed decision

Maintain a distribution manifest identifying the management product, tenant, runtime image, chart, support channel, endpoint set and enabled flags. Evaluate OSS source only as evidence for the selected OSS artifact. Require vendor confirmation for commercial runtime and SCM capability parity. Keep beta or body-forwarding modes outside the default governed contract until separately qualified. Do not prescribe the latest publicly observed changelog entry as automatically supported production software.

Consequences and tradeoffs

The manifest prevents false parity assumptions but increases qualification effort across multiple deployment variants. Fewer approved variants reduce maintenance cost. Customers depend on vendor-provided release evidence where source is private.

Required validation

Compare declared and deployed versions and flags, run the negative-control suite on each supported variant, and obtain a current compatibility/support statement. Demonstrate that an unqualified mode cannot be enabled by ordinary callers.

Acceptance gates: PK-T01, PK-T02, PK-T03, PK-T23. Status: not executed.

PK-ADR-003Publish a bounded endpoint and execution-mode contractProposed
AreaArchitecture & trustSuggested ownerApplication platform ownerDrafted7 October 2026

Context

A unified URL can conceal native and translated paths with different persistence, tools, errors and event semantics. Applications need a stable contract stronger than request acceptance. Security-sensitive options must never disappear unnoticed during adaptation.

Options considered

  • Expose every documented route and pass through new parameters.
  • Publish a minimal tested contract and expand through acceptance gates.
  • Use provider-native APIs exclusively.

Proposed decision

Publish approved API/provider/mode combinations with required fields, unsupported-field disposition, resource semantics and denial classification. Start with bounded chat and separately qualified streaming. Distinguish native Responses from stateless adapted Responses. Forbid client-selected Nitro, beta, custom-destination and debugging modes unless explicitly allowed by a dedicated contract. Reject or deliberately classify unsupported security/retention options rather than treating successful parsing as compatibility.

Consequences and tradeoffs

Some provider features will remain inaccessible through the shared route until tested. The restriction reduces accidental behavior changes and makes migration feasible. Application teams must own fixtures for their semantic and quality requirements.

Required validation

Test required fields, tools, structured output, native errors, ignored options, streaming events and stored-resource methods against native and proxied control groups. Include client libraries that discard unknown events.

PK-ADR-004Version model contracts independently of provider referencesProposed
AreaArchitecture & trustSuggested ownerModel platform ownerDrafted7 October 2026

Context

Applications benefit from a stable model promise, but a provider slug or catalog listing is only an address and access reference. Changing the selected deployment can alter context limits, tools, quality, location, state and price without changing the application request shape.

Options considered

  • Let applications select arbitrary catalog models.
  • Publish reviewed model contracts mapped to approved targets.
  • Hardcode one physical provider deployment in every application.

Proposed decision

Maintain an organization-owned catalog of model contracts, mapping each to approved physical targets, provider accounts, locations, capabilities and evaluation evidence. Define who can change that mapping and when a new contract version is required. Use catalog provisioning and locked configs to enforce access, but retain the contract outside the vendor UI. Require explicit requalification for embedding-model or stateful-provider changes.

Consequences and tradeoffs

The abstraction improves portability only when the mapping is governed. It adds evaluation and release work, and an application may need more than one contract rather than a universal alias. Broad provider access remains a deliberate exception.

Required validation

Prove forbidden model and newly added integration access is denied. Replace a target in a canary and verify schema, semantic quality, location, usage and resource compatibility before promotion.

PK-ADR-005Issue distinct least-privilege workload keysProposed
AreaArchitecture & trustSuggested ownerIdentity platform ownerDrafted7 October 2026

Context

Shared keys erase attribution and make revocation disruptive. A key with valid authentication can still carry more authority than the workload needs. Human development, unattended services and administration have different accountability and lifecycle requirements.

Options considered

  • Share a workspace or organization credential.
  • Create distinct scoped service identities per application/environment.
  • Use short-lived delegated assertions for all traffic where supported.

Proposed decision

Assign each workload and environment a named, owned credential with the smallest verified operation scope, explicit workspace/model grants and a documented expiry/rotation process. Keep human and automation identities separate. Deny policy, provider, prompt, log and key administration unless separately justified. Attach and lock the required request policy. Preserve service attribution even when user identity is propagated for business authorization.

Consequences and tradeoffs

More credentials require provisioning automation and lifecycle ownership, but compromise and revocation can be contained. A workload key remains a service authority rather than proof of the current end user; applications need a separate user authorization mechanism.

Required validation

Exercise every forbidden management method and another workspace, then rotate and revoke through all serving nodes. Measure the actual revocation window, including warm operation under management outage.

Acceptance gates: PK-T03, PK-T04, PK-T06, PK-T14. Status: not executed.

Revisit trigger

A new workload, shared credential, delegated user model or ownership change appears.

PK-ADR-006Validate JWT trust, intended use and revocation explicitlyProposed
AreaArchitecture & trustSuggested ownerIdentity security ownerDrafted7 October 2026

Context

Token signatures establish a signer, not the correct tenant, audience, policy or business permission. Local validation and caches introduce lifecycle behavior that differs from database-backed key lookup. Gateway access assertions and downstream tool assertions are separate trust relationships.

Options considered

  • Accept any token signed by a configured key.
  • Validate a constrained claim contract at the gateway and supporting identity broker.
  • Use scoped opaque keys until required JWT behavior is proven.

Proposed decision

Approve exact signer/algorithm, issuer, intended recipient, expiry, organization, workspace and scope mappings. Test the gateway behavior rather than assuming omitted controls are enforced. Ensure missing or unresolved required policy context fails closed through a demonstrated mechanism. Use bounded token lifetimes and a measured emergency revocation path. For tool forwarding, verify the downstream trust and business-object permissions separately from gateway authentication.

Consequences and tradeoffs

An identity broker or backend validation layer may be needed when native claims behavior does not satisfy the contract. Short lifetimes increase identity-service dependency, while long lifetimes increase stale-authority exposure. Neither tradeoff should be hidden behind an SSO checkbox.

Required validation

Use validly signed but wrongly scoped tokens, stale signing keys, wrong tenants and missing config claims. Test cold and warm nodes during rotation and management loss. Record the last accepted revoked assertion.

Acceptance gates: PK-T05, PK-T07, PK-T14, PK-T19. Status: not executed.

Revisit trigger

Trust provider, claim schema, validation mode, token lifetime or tool delegation changes.

PK-ADR-007Make tenant and resource isolation a tested invariantProposed
AreaArchitecture & trustSuggested ownerSecurity architectDrafted7 October 2026

Context

Workspaces organize policy but do not prove every resource method is tenant-safe. Cache results, provider files, task identifiers, logs and future model provisioning create additional access surfaces. Client-supplied metadata cannot authenticate ownership.

Options considered

  • Rely on workspace labels alone.
  • Prove logical isolation across all resource and execution surfaces.
  • Use separate organizations/runtime stacks for stronger boundaries.

Proposed decision

Derive tenant identity from verified credentials or an approved mapping and intersect it with model, tool and resource grants. Bind every stored handle to owner, workspace, provider account and location. Test read/list/delete as rigorously as invocation. Namespace caches from trusted context. Use separate organizations, credentials or runtimes where logical tests or contractual guarantees do not meet the required isolation strength.

Consequences and tradeoffs

Owner indexes and negative tests add application work, but they expose gaps that feature checklists miss. Physical separation costs more and does not remove the need for resource authorization. New-workspace and inherited-access behavior must be reviewed continuously.

Required validation

Run a cross-tenant corpus across model calls, metadata spoofing, cache hits, logs, files, jobs, MCP tools and A2A tasks. Create new integrations/workspaces and verify no accidental privilege expansion.

PK-ADR-008Separate management authority from inference trafficProposed
AreaArchitecture & trustSuggested ownerSecurity operations ownerDrafted7 October 2026

Context

Policy writers and administrators can change destinations, credentials, safety behavior and retained data. They therefore hold a stronger authority than an ordinary inference caller. Private networking helps reduce exposure but does not establish least privilege or attributable changes.

Options considered

  • Use one administration credential and common public route.
  • Separate named management roles, automation and network exposure.
  • Delegate all configuration to application workspaces.

Proposed decision

Restrict managed administration and customer management endpoints to approved operators and automation. Separate policy approval, credential administration and runtime operation where feasible. Use named service accounts, time-bounded emergency access and protected audit export. Do not expose log retrieval, registration or diagnostics through inference wildcards. Review workspace delegation for changes that alter organizational security or privacy requirements.

Consequences and tradeoffs

Administrative work may require review and slower promotion. That cost buys attributable changes and smaller compromise scope. Managed-console availability and vendor administrator controls remain contractual dependencies requiring explicit evidence.

Required validation

Attempt management operations with application credentials and from the application network. Execute representative approved and denied UI/API changes and reconstruct who changed what, when and with which effective result.

PK-ADR-009Separate provider secrets, encryption and registration authorityProposed
AreaArchitecture & trustSuggested ownerSecrets platform ownerDrafted7 October 2026

Context

The runtime may hold provider credentials, vault permissions, scan-service keys and signed-identity material. Encryption protects stored objects but does not remove the runtime permission to decrypt or use them. Credential caching and workspace scoping affect rotation and recovery.

Options considered

  • Store shared secrets directly in broad configuration.
  • Use scoped secret references and separately managed encryption/signing material.
  • Use provider workload identities wherever the integration supports them.

Proposed decision

Prefer constrained workload identities or runtime secret resolution, with explicit workspace access and audited vault permissions. Keep provider, scan, management, registration, encryption and MCP signing authorities distinct. Define cache-aware rotation and emergency revocation at the source provider as well as the gateway. Confirm actual KMS principals for the deployment; never copy a hosted example blindly. Exclude plaintext secrets from manifests, logs and diagnostic exports.

Consequences and tradeoffs

More identities and key lifecycles increase operational complexity. Vault or KMS availability can become a request dependency, and cached secrets can outlive a central change. Those dependencies must be measured rather than hidden by an encrypted-at-rest claim.

Required validation

Rotate and revoke under load, deny fetch/decrypt access, cold-start nodes and exercise failover. Confirm no unrelated workspace can resolve a secret and no secret values appear in configured sinks.

PK-ADR-010Bind egress and processing location to the complete routeProposed
AreaArchitecture & trustSuggested ownerNetwork and privacy ownersDrafted7 October 2026

Context

An approved model destination is only one recipient in a composed gateway request. Scanners, tools, metadata, log viewing and secret services add paths. Hybrid runtime placement alone cannot establish end-to-end residency or prevent credential forwarding to an unintended host.

Options considered

  • Allow arbitrary provider URLs and rely on application discipline.
  • Allowlist the complete execution graph and credential recipient.
  • Use fully isolated single-provider stacks for constrained workloads.

Proposed decision

Approve model, scanner, tool, secret, management and telemetry destinations by workload and data class. Restrict custom hosts, redirects, DNS/private-address changes and forwarded credential headers through tested gateway and network controls. Apply the same policy to retries and fallbacks. Record processing and retention requirements separately. Do not route a required scan or tool call to another region merely to recover availability without an approved exception.

Consequences and tradeoffs

Explicit egress can slow provider onboarding and requires maintenance as service endpoints change. It makes data movement explainable and limits SSRF/credential leakage exposure. Network controls alone cannot authorize a business object or prove provider retention behavior.

Required validation

Use controlled destination tests, redirect chains and unexpected provider headers; observe actual traffic and credentials. Verify the full graph for native, adapted, cached, tool and failure paths.

PK-ADR-011Route only among approved equivalent targetsProposed
AreaExecution & stateSuggested ownerRuntime platform ownerDrafted7 October 2026

Context

Pooling capacity and changing the model contract are different decisions. A router can return a valid response while violating required capabilities, quality, processing location or resource ownership. Adaptive behavior is harder to explain than a small static target set.

Options considered

  • Expose arbitrary provider fallback.
  • Begin with explicit weighted/equivalent targets and bounded fallback.
  • Adopt adaptive optimization immediately.

Proposed decision

Start with a small reviewed target graph and deterministic eligibility rules. Each primary and backup must meet the same approved workload contract, including model capability, credentials, location, quality and output limits. Use circuit state as a health signal, not an authorization bypass. Promote adaptive or conditional policies only with separate failure-distribution and task-quality evidence. Record the actual target per attempt.

Consequences and tradeoffs

The eligible pool may be smaller and more expensive than every technically callable model. The restriction reduces surprising substitutions and makes incidents explainable. Stateful resources may remain pinned even when stateless inference can move.

Required validation

Simulate every failure branch, throttling, cooldown and recovery. Confirm that denied, incompatible or location-prohibited targets receive no work. Compare application quality on all permitted alternatives.

PK-ADR-012Give one layer ownership of retries and deadlinesProposed
AreaExecution & stateSuggested ownerApplication reliability ownerDrafted7 October 2026

Context

Client, gateway and provider libraries can all retry. Their combined behavior may exceed the intended duration or financial exposure. A network failure after dispatch is ambiguous, and replaying tool or job operations can duplicate side effects.

Options considered

  • Leave retries enabled independently at each layer.
  • Assign one retry owner with bounded total attempts and wall time.
  • Disable all retries and rely on caller recovery.

Proposed decision

Define the single retry owner per workload, the retryable failure classes, maximum total attempts and end-to-end deadline. Account for upstream/client hidden retries and Retry-After behavior. Stop on authentication or terminal policy denial. Preserve the remaining deadline through fallback. Treat ambiguous dispatch as potentially completed and billable. Require domain idempotency or explicit reconciliation before replaying side-effecting operations.

Consequences and tradeoffs

Some failures surface to users rather than being hidden by another attempt. The policy reduces amplification and makes cost/exposure predictable. Applications need clear incomplete/unknown outcomes and recovery guidance instead of a generic retry-on-error wrapper.

Required validation

Trace all actual attempts under connection drops, timeouts, throttling and fallback. Prove no replay after partial disclosure or unverified side effects, and verify the full deadline at the client boundary.

Acceptance gates: PK-T09, PK-T10, PK-T11, PK-T15, PK-T20. Status: not executed.

Revisit trigger

Client SDK, provider behavior, fallback graph or transaction semantics changes.

PK-ADR-013Specify streaming, cancellation and disclosure explicitlyProposed
AreaExecution & stateSuggested ownerApplication ownerDrafted7 October 2026

Context

A stream creates an irreversible disclosure boundary before final usage or safety results may arrive. Client libraries differ in handling gateway-added events. Closing a connection cannot be assumed to stop provider computation or remove financial exposure.

Options considered

  • Treat streaming like an ordinary successful HTTP response.
  • Publish a stream lifecycle with bounded timing and explicit incomplete outcomes.
  • Use non-streaming buffered responses for the initial supported contract.

Proposed decision

Define first-byte, idle and absolute-duration limits, supported events, partial tool handling, final usage and terminal outcome classification. Verify client-visible denials independently of HTTP status. Do not retry after emitted content as a transparent continuation. Record cancellation attempts and unknown upstream completion. Use buffered delivery or disallow the workload when preventive output inspection is required but not demonstrated on the streaming path.

Consequences and tradeoffs

Buffering may reduce interactivity and increase memory. Explicit incomplete outcomes require application UX and accounting work. The design prevents a late diagnostic event from being misrepresented as prevention and separates transport success from task completion.

Required validation

Interrupt before dispatch, before first chunk, during content/tool arguments and before final usage. Test each supported SDK and raw protocol client; compare what was delivered with recorded policy and usage outcomes.

Revisit trigger

Streaming API, client parser, timeout policy, output inspection or tool protocol changes.

PK-ADR-014Require preventive controls by route and execution phaseProposed
AreaExecution & stateSuggested ownerAI safety and security ownersDrafted7 October 2026

Context

Input checks, output checks, asynchronous observation and external security scans protect different boundaries. A configured hook may be optional, overridden, late or unavailable in a special mode. Marketing descriptions cannot establish the exact prevention guarantee.

Options considered

  • Attach generic guardrails and accept defaults.
  • Define required preventive checks and qualify their execution per route.
  • Use detective monitoring only with explicit residual-risk acceptance.

Proposed decision

Version each required check with its phase, covered content, verdict/action schema, permitted data recipient and timeout/failure policy. Lock mandatory policy against caller and workspace bypass. Prevent upstream dispatch or client disclosure only through a demonstrated synchronous/buffering mechanism. Label asynchronous or post-stream checks detective. PK-ADR-015Keep exact response caching opt-in and tenant-safeProposed
AreaExecution & stateSuggested ownerData platform ownerDrafted7 October 2026

Context

Answer reuse can reduce work but also disclose data or preserve obsolete policy outcomes. Authentication, namespace partitioning and content key construction are separate mechanisms. Provider-owned resources and side effects are not ordinary reusable answers.

Options considered

  • Cache all successful completions by default.
  • Enable exact caching only for explicitly eligible workloads.
  • Avoid gateway response caching entirely.

Proposed decision

Default response caching off. For an approved workload, authenticate and resolve policy before reuse; derive a trusted namespace including tenant and relevant model/policy/data version; bound TTL and content retention. Do not accept arbitrary caller namespaces. Exclude secrets, personalized authorization-sensitive results, provider-owned handles and side effects. Define invalidation and cost reporting for hits independently of control-object caching.

Consequences and tradeoffs

Hit rate may be lower than broad shared caching and some workloads receive no benefit. This preserves confidentiality and traceability. Namespace/version changes are part of release management, and cache deletion does not erase other recipients or historical logs.

Required validation

Use identical prompts across tenants and changing permissions/model versions. Verify no cross-owner hits, correct expiry and invalidation, reauthorization and cost interpretation. Test unsupported streaming combinations explicitly.

AreaExecution & stateSuggested ownerApplication product ownerDrafted7 October 2026

Context

Similarity-based answer reuse can return a plausible but task-inappropriate result. It may also introduce an embedding service and another data store. A good exact-cache result provides no evidence that semantic matching preserves correctness for a regulated or transactional task.

Options considered

  • Enable semantic caching wherever exact caching is available.
  • Evaluate it per task against a versioned corpus and explicit risk threshold.
  • Limit the service to exact or no caching.

Proposed decision

Keep semantic caching out of the initial shared contract. Admit it only for a named workload after testing task correctness, tenant isolation, sensitivity, freshness and the additional embedding/storage recipients. Set acceptance thresholds from business consequences rather than generic similarity scores. Exclude authorization decisions, exact extraction obligations and side-effecting tasks unless a separate authoritative validation step makes reuse safe.

Consequences and tradeoffs

Potential savings are deferred and a task-specific evaluation is required. Semantic cache operation becomes part of the product, with drift, invalidation and quality ownership. The organization can decline it even when the gateway supports the feature.

Required validation

Compare against an uncached control using near-duplicate, contradictory, stale and cross-tenant prompts. Measure false reuse and downstream corrections as well as hit rate, latency and total cost.

Acceptance gates: PK-T06, PK-T13, PK-T24. Status: not executed.

Revisit trigger

Task, corpus, embedding model, similarity settings or error tolerance changes.

PK-ADR-017Preserve managed desired state and customer recovery evidenceProposed
AreaExecution & stateSuggested ownerPlatform architectDrafted7 October 2026

Context

The original reference concern required a durable governance authority. In commercial Portkey/SCM, that authority is a managed service rather than a customer PostgreSQL deployment. Cached runtime objects are not a sufficient backup, and private vendor persistence internals are not public evidence.

Options considered

  • Treat runtime cache as the configuration system of record.
  • Use managed desired state with controlled customer exports and release evidence.
  • Adopt a fully customer-operated distribution under a separate contract.

Proposed decision

Recognize the selected managed control plane as the serving configuration authority while retaining customer-owned approved declarations, dependency maps and export evidence. Define conflict and drift ownership between reviewed source and managed objects. Contract for export, recovery, deletion and incident support. Keep business resource ownership and any strict monetary ledger in explicitly owned durable systems. Do not invent an unsupported customer database layer to emulate the managed product.

Consequences and tradeoffs

Managed persistence reduces infrastructure work but introduces vendor recovery dependence and export limitations. Customer evidence supports reconstruction and exit but must not silently override emergency changes. Cache continuity remains a separate operational feature.

Required validation

Reconstruct a test tenant/runtime from approved exports, verify dependency order and effective policy, and document objects or histories that require vendor action. Test loss of local caches without losing authoritative declarations.

PK-ADR-018Separate coordination and configuration from answer cachingProposed
AreaExecution & stateSuggested ownerSRE ownerDrafted7 October 2026

Context

Runtime caches may hold governance objects, pending usage and optional answer data with very different failure consequences. Configuring one Redis endpoint does not prove that all clients share the needed state or that multiple enforcement domains have globally consistent counters.

Options considered

  • Use one undifferentiated cache and accept defaults.
  • Document logical state classes and qualify the supported shared topology.
  • Use isolated runtimes with explicit independent allowances.

Proposed decision

Inventory each cache/counter client, key namespace, TTL, eviction policy, acknowledgement and failure response. Keep response-cache eligibility separate from coordination and configuration availability. Use vendor-supported shared state and capacity, with isolation where justified. Test stale restoration and local fallback rather than assuming limits remain correct. Specify maximum authorization/configuration age independently of cache retention and ensure pending accounting state has an explicit loss/replay contract.

Consequences and tradeoffs

Extra state isolation or capacity can add cost. The documentation burden exposes hidden dependencies and allows security, availability and financial tradeoffs to be reviewed separately. No global atomicity claim is made from a common Redis label.

Required validation

Inject memory pressure, partitions, cache loss, stale snapshots, new nodes and restarts during usage flush. Measure admitted work, revocation convergence, duplicates, gaps and cold-object behavior.

Cache topology, scaling domain, TTL, eviction, resync or failure policy changes.

PK-ADR-019Distinguish native allowances from strict monetary admissionProposed
AreaExecution & stateSuggested ownerFinOps and service ownersDrafted7 October 2026

Context

Operational rate/budget policies can be valuable without constituting an exact dispatch-time spending ceiling. Concurrency, delayed usage, retries, tool work, unknown prices and regional separation create exposure. Financial correctness must be specified before selecting a mechanism.

Options considered

  • Treat configured usage budgets as an unconditional cap.
  • Accept native approximate allowances with a documented exposure bound.
  • Add a separately qualified reservation/admission service for strict requirements.

Proposed decision

Classify each workload as ordinary allowance or strict monetary authorization. Use native policies where their tested contract is sufficient. For strict scope, reserve a conservative approved maximum before dispatch using idempotent request/attempt records, bound unknown exposure and fail closed when authority is unverifiable. Include retries, auxiliary services and asynchronous work. Do not release a reservation solely on client disconnect or absence of usage. Keep the stronger mechanism explicitly customer-owned unless vendor evidence establishes it.

Consequences and tradeoffs

Strict admission adds state, estimation and availability costs and may reject useful work. Native limits remain useful defense in depth. Exact invoice matching may still be impossible when upstream billing is delayed or nondeterministic, so the accepted guarantee must be precisely bounded.

Required validation

Run parallel near-limit requests, regional partitions, unknown-price routes, crashes and partial streams. Demonstrate reservation settlement, exception ownership and the maximum accepted overshoot/exposure.

Acceptance gates: PK-T10, PK-T14, PK-T15, PK-T16. Status: not executed.

Revisit trigger

Financial requirement, pricing basis, concurrency, regions or chargeable feature set changes.

PK-ADR-020Reconcile application, provider and gateway ledgers separatelyProposed
AreaExecution & stateSuggested ownerFinOps ownerDrafted7 October 2026

Context

An application request can create several model attempts, scan calls and tool transactions. Provider usage and gateway commercial metering are different units, while control-plane reporting may arrive later. Collapsing them hides discrepancies and can double charge internal users.

Options considered

  • Use the gateway dashboard as the sole ledger.
  • Maintain a customer attempt ledger and reconcile each billing authority.
  • Accept aggregate organizational billing without request chargeback.

Proposed decision

Record logical request and actual attempt identifiers, tenant, target, policy/pricing revision, measured or estimated usage, result class and uncertainty. Reconcile application reservations against attempts, attempts against provider billing dimensions, and gateway-metered usage against the commercial invoice. Use idempotent ingestion and exception queues for missing/duplicate events. Label character-derived tool metering distinctly from tokenizer output. Do not invent an exact request-ID invoice join where the supplier does not provide one.

Consequences and tradeoffs

A separate ledger adds retention and data-engineering responsibility. It improves explainability and internal chargeback but cannot manufacture missing upstream facts. Metadata should be minimized and access restricted to legitimate finance/operations roles.

Required validation

Reconcile known fixtures containing cache hits, retries, partial streams, errors, scans, batches and agent/tool calls. Simulate failed flushes and duplicate events, then resolve each discrepancy with preserved evidence.

Revisit trigger

Billing unit, price model, event schema, attribution policy or provider invoice granularity changes.

PK-ADR-021Make effective configuration ownership explicitProposed
AreaDelivery & operationsSuggested ownerRelease engineering ownerDrafted7 October 2026

Context

A saved config, a key default, workspace delegation and caller parameters can all influence one request. A reviewed object name does not prove which effective policy executed. Managed UI convenience should not create an untracked second source of security-sensitive changes.

Options considered

  • Allow free runtime edits and caller overrides.
  • Assign reviewed ownership with limited delegation and effective-policy verification.
  • Make all configuration immutable and prohibit emergency changes.

Proposed decision

Assign an owner to every security-sensitive field and object. Promote reviewed configs, model mappings, guards, logging and egress rules through a controlled process, with exact content/version evidence. Disable unapproved caller overrides and restrict workspace delegation. Permit audited emergency changes under a defined reconciliation procedure. Verify the effective configuration on serving nodes; do not infer it from a successful UI save or a mutable config slug.

Consequences and tradeoffs

Changes require review and may converge asynchronously. Emergency operations need a clear reconciliation owner. The approach preserves developer flexibility for explicitly delegated settings while preventing policy drift from being mistaken for intended behavior.

Required validation

Change defaults, workspace rules and explicit request fields in conflicting combinations. Verify the accepted precedence, denied bypasses, effective revisions and exported change evidence across all runtimes.

Configuration schema, precedence, default settings, delegation or management product changes.

PK-ADR-022Promote coherent releases with a bounded rollback pathProposed
AreaDelivery & operationsSuggested ownerRelease managerDrafted7 October 2026

Context

Gateway binaries, managed objects, model APIs, client libraries and feature flags evolve independently. A container rollback alone may not restore the accepted contract, and it cannot undo provider billing, retained data or tool side effects.

Options considered

  • Upgrade runtime images independently whenever available.
  • Release a tested artifact/configuration/client contract set with canary and rollback.
  • Freeze indefinitely on an observed version.

Proposed decision

Record the vendor-confirmed runtime/chart support set, image digests, managed policy revisions, model mappings, credentials by reference, client contracts and feature flags as one release. Test in isolation, canary bounded workloads, compare actual behavior and drain before broader promotion. Keep compatible prior artifacts and owner mappings until the rollback window closes. Define which managed changes are reversible and which require forward repair or vendor assistance.

Consequences and tradeoffs

Qualification takes effort and may delay optional features. It reduces accidental version skew and makes incident recovery deliberate. Freezing is not a security strategy; patch intake and model/API lifecycle events still require active review.

Required validation

Rehearse a failed canary, configuration rollback, key rotation during upgrade and interrupted jobs/streams. Verify no permission broadening, stranded resources or unaccounted work when returning to the accepted state.

PK-ADR-023Choose deployment separation for explicit failure and trust boundariesProposed
AreaDelivery & operationsSuggested ownerPlatform architectDrafted7 October 2026

Context

SaaS, hybrid and separated protocol pools allocate different responsibilities. More services can isolate resource pressure and credentials, but also add costs, licensing questions and operational interfaces. The management product remains a distinct dependency even when runtimes are customer-operated.

Options considered

  • One shared deployment for all protocols and environments.
  • Separate only the pools needed for security or workload isolation.
  • Fully isolate every application and dependency.

Proposed decision

Select SaaS or hybrid based on contractual management, network and runtime-placement requirements. Within customer-operated scope, separate production from development and isolate LLM, tool or agent pools when their credentials, egress or long-lived resource demands justify it. Document shared control-plane, cache and telemetry dependencies. Do not describe a physical split as complete independence without tests. Obtain explicit entitlement for the intended number and topology of deployments.

Consequences and tradeoffs

Separation can reduce blast radius and noisy-neighbor effects but increases infrastructure, upgrades and support complexity. A shared managed plane can remain a correlated failure/security domain. Simpler deployments are preferable when they meet the requirements.

Required validation

Saturate or compromise a simulated protocol pool and verify other workloads remain within their contract. Map all shared dependencies and test the management outage behavior of each pool.

PK-ADR-024Bound concurrency, connection pools and autoscaling togetherProposed
AreaDelivery & operationsSuggested ownerSRE capacity ownerDrafted7 October 2026

Context

Requests-per-second alone does not size long streams, media, scans and agent tasks. Scaling runtimes also changes connections to providers, caches and secret services. Unbounded queues hide overload until deadlines expire and retries multiply the work.

Options considered

  • Scale on CPU alone with large queues.
  • Use workload-specific concurrency and dependency-aware scaling.
  • Provision fixed peak capacity and reject excess traffic.

Proposed decision

Define workload classes with maximum bytes, output size, active requests, queue delay and lifetime. Bound connection pools and auxiliary calls, then scale within tested provider/cache/vault capacity. Use client-observed latency and rejection metrics alongside CPU/memory. Shed or reject overload early with a documented recovery signal. Keep retry and financial admission limits in effect during autoscaling and avoid admitting more work simply because another pod starts.

Consequences and tradeoffs

Early rejection is visible to clients and requires retry guidance. Capacity headroom and isolation cost money, but uncontrolled buffering and provider amplification are less predictable. Per-class metrics and realistic burst tests are necessary operational work.

Required validation

Load-test mixed short calls, long streams, slow scans, large inputs and jobs. Observe queue age, pool wait, memory, sockets, dependency saturation and policy correctness during scaling and draining.

Revisit trigger

Workload duration, payload size, provider quotas, scan latency or scaling topology changes.

PK-ADR-025Default to minimized telemetry and qualify every failure pathProposed
AreaDelivery & operationsSuggested ownerPrivacy and observability ownersDrafted7 October 2026

Context

Observability is valuable, but prompts, transformed output, URLs, metadata and error bodies can contain sensitive data. A setting named metrics-only is not evidence that all protocols and failures exclude content. Local log storage may still be remotely viewable.

Options considered

  • Capture complete payloads for all requests.
  • Use minimized metadata by default with approved time-bounded content capture.
  • Disable all telemetry, including accounting and operational evidence.

Proposed decision

Define an allowed telemetry schema per sink and protocol. Default to bounded metadata, protect tenant identifiers and lock organizational logging controls where required. Allow content capture only for named purposes, restricted access and retention. Test errors, tool outputs and transformed/original content separately. Bound exporter queues and distinguish optional diagnostics from required audit/accounting evidence. Record dashboard access paths and verify historical deletion independently of future capture settings.

Consequences and tradeoffs

Some incidents will be harder to debug without payloads and require controlled synthetic reproduction. Minimized metadata still needs privacy review. Telemetry outages need explicit degraded behavior so performance is not protected by silently losing required evidence.

Required validation

Inject synthetic secrets into successful and failed model/tool calls, inspect every sink and UI path, then test collector saturation, duplicate delivery, retention expiry and historical purge.

PK-ADR-028Separate health, readiness, freshness and graceful drainingProposed
AreaDelivery & operationsSuggested ownerSRE ownerDrafted7 October 2026

Context

A running process can lack usable credentials or configuration for a cold route. A healthy cached route can still violate the accepted authorization freshness. Long streams and jobs also outlive ordinary HTTP health checks and deployment shutdown windows.

Options considered

  • Use one process-health endpoint for every readiness decision.
  • Define separate liveness, contract readiness, freshness and drain states.
  • Probe all downstream services synchronously on every health request.

Proposed decision

Keep liveness simple and non-destructive. Define readiness for the supported workload class, including required config/secret availability and accepted freshness. Avoid probes that consume billable inference or create cascading outages without need. On shutdown, stop admitting new work, retain completion/accounting paths for accepted work and drain within a bounded period. Classify interrupted streams and durable jobs explicitly rather than treating pod termination as successful cancellation.

Consequences and tradeoffs

Readiness is more nuanced than an HTTP 200 and can differ for warm and cold paths. Conservative admission may reduce availability during management incidents. Clear drain and freshness metrics improve safe rollout and prevent silent stale-authority operation.

Required validation

Cold-start with unavailable management/vault/cache, then test warm state, expired objects and a revoked key. Terminate under streams/jobs and prove outcomes, usage and resource ownership remain explainable.

Revisit trigger

Health checks, configuration cache behavior, workload duration or orchestration lifecycle changes.

PK-ADR-029Establish multi-zone resilience before regional expansionProposed
AreaDelivery & operationsSuggested ownerSRE and platform architectsDrafted7 October 2026

Context

Additional regions introduce new model capacity, credentials, configuration paths, policy propagation and financial domains. A global traffic switch can mask unresolved state and location constraints. Most initial resilience work should establish a dependable single-region service first.

Options considered

  • Deploy globally from the first pilot.
  • Prove multi-zone operation, then add regions for explicit requirements.
  • Run one instance and rely on vendor/provider availability.

Proposed decision

For customer-operated scope, qualify multi-zone runtime and supported state dependencies before adding a second region. Document correlated managed-plane, secret, provider and telemetry failures. Add a region only for an approved continuity or processing-location need, with compatible targets and owner-bound resource recovery. Failover destinations must satisfy the original policy and capacity contract. Test warm and cold recovery, not only load-balancer health switching.

Consequences and tradeoffs

Regional rollout is delayed and some rare outages remain initially out of scope. The staged approach avoids multiplying untested dependencies. Vendor SaaS resilience must be established by contract and observable evidence rather than inferred from a customer topology diagram.

Required validation

Lose a zone, node pool and dependency independently, then perform a region-level exercise after prerequisites pass. Verify authorization, routing location, usage and retained-resource continuity throughout.

PK-ADR-030Allocate quotas and monetary exposure by enforcement domainProposed
AreaDelivery & operationsSuggested ownerFinOps and reliability ownersDrafted7 October 2026

Context

A policy named global may be enforced through distributed runtime state whose partition behavior must be verified. Regional failure can lead both regions to accept work against stale totals. Restoring an old counter snapshot can also lower apparent usage without lowering the bill.

Options considered

  • Assume all replicas share an instantaneous global counter.
  • Allocate bounded regional allowances and reconcile them.
  • Use a separately qualified strongly coordinated admission service.

Proposed decision

Identify each native enforcement domain and test its consistency. For strict scope, either use an approved global reservation service or allocate bounded regional exposure with controlled reallocation. Never increase available allowance merely by restoring stale state or adding a region. Define reset windows, currency/pricing assumptions and partition behavior. Treat native counters and reports as evidence inputs rather than proof of a stronger global guarantee.

Consequences and tradeoffs

Regional allocation can leave capacity unused while another region is constrained. Strong coordination adds latency and availability dependencies. Both are legitimate tradeoffs when the accepted financial and continuity contracts are explicit.

Required validation

Submit synchronized requests in multiple regions, partition their coordination, reset periods and restore old state. Show total admitted exposure remains within the agreed bound and all discrepancies reconcile afterward.

PK-ADR-031Recover configuration, ownership, accounting and keys togetherProposed
AreaAssurance & exitSuggested ownerRecovery service ownerDrafted7 October 2026

Context

A runtime can be recreated yet still lack valid policy, provider resource ownership or the ability to decrypt stored state. Restoring obsolete grants or credentials can turn disaster recovery into a security regression. Managed persistence also limits what customers can restore independently.

Options considered

  • Restore only containers and Redis snapshots.
  • Recover an approved dependency-ordered service bundle.
  • Rely solely on vendor support with no customer reconstruction evidence.

Proposed decision

Define recovery bundles for approved declarations, managed exports, runtime artifacts, secret/encryption references, protected audit, resource-owner indexes and required financial state. Record vendor-managed recovery dependencies and acceptable loss/recovery objectives. Restore authority and mappings before reopening ingress; do not resurrect revoked credentials. Reconcile uncertain in-flight work and stale counters. Verify data deletion and retention requirements still hold after recovery.

Consequences and tradeoffs

Complete recovery requires coordination across security, application, finance, SRE and vendor teams. Backup scope and encryption-key availability create operational cost. A successful infrastructure restore is intentionally insufficient evidence of a recovered service.

Required validation

Perform a cold rebuild after key rotation and policy changes, recover jobs and logs, and verify negative permissions before allowing traffic. Demonstrate which components cannot be restored without vendor action and test that escalation.

Acceptance gates: PK-T07, PK-T14, PK-T18, PK-T20, PK-T21, PK-T22. Status: not executed.

Revisit trigger

State ownership, encryption, export format, retention or continuity objectives change.

PK-ADR-032Verify artifact provenance and maintain an active patch processProposed
AreaAssurance & exitSuggested ownerPlatform security ownerDrafted7 October 2026

Context

Gateways process provider secrets and untrusted payloads, so dependency and image changes carry security impact. OSS tags, commercial releases and managed tenant updates provide different evidence. An old stable-looking installation example is not a current support or vulnerability guarantee.

Options considered

  • Use moving image tags and trust upstream packaging.
  • Pin approved artifacts and verify available provenance/security evidence.
  • Fork and maintain all runtime dependencies internally.

Proposed decision

Record exact image and chart digests, source/release identity where available, supported platform matrix, available signatures/attestations/SBOMs and accepted exceptions. Verify commercial evidence with the vendor rather than substituting OSS source. Maintain vulnerability and release intake with emergency qualification focused on authentication, destination validation, credentials, tools and resource methods. Avoid unsupported freezes; keep a tested rollback or forward-repair plan.

Consequences and tradeoffs

Verification and patch qualification consume engineering effort and may reveal gaps in vendor evidence. The response to missing attestations must be an explicit risk decision. A private image does not remove responsibility to evaluate its deployment and supported lifecycle.

Required validation

Prove deployed digest matches approval, scan the actual artifact, rehearse an urgent update and verify the controls did not regress. Test that deployment automation refuses an unapproved artifact or reports a governed exception.

Runtime, dependency, packaging channel, vulnerability or supported platform changes.

PK-ADR-033Control plugins, callbacks and custom routes as privileged codeProposed
AreaAssurance & exitSuggested ownerPlatform security architectDrafted7 October 2026

Context

An integration can inspect content, invoke networks, access secrets or alter execution even when described as logging or a guardrail. Configuration can also create fan-out or redirect provider credentials. Extensibility therefore expands both the trusted computing base and the data-flow graph.

Options considered

  • Allow workspace-defined plugins and custom hosts freely.
  • Approve a constrained extension catalog with bounded authority.
  • Prohibit all non-core integrations.

Proposed decision

Maintain an approved inventory of callbacks, plugins, custom destinations and beta execution paths. Assign each an owner, purpose, credential scope, permitted data, egress, timeout, resource budget and failure policy. Review executable changes as code, and configuration changes as policy programs. Prevent ordinary workloads from registering arbitrary extensions. Validate output from external services rather than trusting it as control instructions. Require independent release and rollback evidence for security integrations.

Consequences and tradeoffs

Onboarding integrations becomes slower but auditable. Some desired features may need a separate service with stronger isolation. The gateway still depends on its core implementation; restricting extensions reduces rather than eliminates that trust.

Required validation

Cause an integration to stall, return malformed decisions, request forbidden destinations, leak a synthetic credential or fan out excessively. Prove containment and correct request/audit outcomes without broad permission grants.

Plugin code, external service, custom route, feature flag or data recipient changes.

PK-ADR-034Default-deny MCP and authorize tools at the business boundaryProposed
AreaAssurance & exitSuggested ownerTool platform ownerDrafted7 October 2026

Context

Registry access, workspace provisioning, tool enablement, user permission and transaction authorization are distinct. Some retrieved MCP control pages describe forthcoming capabilities. A model-generated tool call cannot be treated as a grant to execute a business action.

Options considered

  • Trust every tool exposed by a provisioned server.
  • Use explicit tool grants plus verified identity and backend authorization.
  • Keep MCP outside the shared gateway until required controls are available.

Proposed decision

Begin with an approved server/tool subset and deny unqualified capabilities. Test both discovery and direct invocation. Forward identity only through an approved verifiable trust path, and require the tool backend to authorize the actual user, resource and action. Bind high-risk approval to exact arguments and enforce domain idempotency. Supply required limits/guardrails independently when not demonstrated by the selected gateway release; do not credit roadmap promises as deployed protection.

Consequences and tradeoffs

Tool services retain meaningful security responsibility and may need an authorization/approval layer. The design limits convenience but prevents registry membership from becoming unrestricted execution. New tool schemas or server behavior require requalification even without gateway changes.

Required validation

Attempt hidden tools directly, forged identity headers, cross-owner objects, replayed writes and chained delegation. Verify missing approvals, limits and invalid arguments stop the action at the backend business boundary.

PK-ADR-035Preserve provider and agent ownership for stateful resourcesProposed
AreaAssurance & exitSuggested ownerApplication data ownerDrafted7 October 2026

Context

Files, stored responses, batch jobs and A2A tasks belong to an upstream account or service context. A generic resource identifier is not sufficient to route or authorize retrieval. Native and adapted API paths may also provide different persistence behavior.

Options considered

  • Route all resource methods through whichever provider is currently selected.
  • Maintain explicit owner/upstream bindings and lifecycle policy.
  • Expose only stateless inference.

Proposed decision

Bind each retained resource to authenticated owner, workspace, provider/agent endpoint, account, region, creation policy and retention deadline in a durable customer index where needed. Authorize list/read/download/delete independently from inference. Preserve the correct route through credential rotation and migration. Disallow generic cross-provider fallback for owner-bound resources. Specify how to resolve ambiguous creation and how deletion is verified in every actual store.

Consequences and tradeoffs

Applications acquire lifecycle and recovery responsibilities that a unified API cannot remove. Resource portability may be limited and migration may require draining rather than copying. Stateless workloads remain simpler and should not inherit unnecessary retained state.

Required validation

Test wrong-owner methods, guessed IDs, key rotation, provider changes, lost callbacks and interrupted create/delete operations. Demonstrate recovery of stranded resources without broadening access or duplicating jobs.

PK-ADR-036Govern batch, media and agent work with separate admissionProposed
AreaAssurance & exitSuggested ownerWorkflow service ownerDrafted7 October 2026

Context

Large uploads, asynchronous jobs and agent loops have different resource and financial profiles from short chat requests. Completion can outlive the gateway connection or rollout. Blind retries and unclear ownership create duplicate work and unbounded side effects.

Options considered

  • Apply ordinary chat limits to every workload.
  • Use separate admission classes and durable orchestration.
  • Keep all long-running work outside the gateway.

Proposed decision

Define byte/object, concurrent job, duration, output, tool-call and financial limits per workload class. Persist owner and upstream IDs before treating submission as complete. Resolve ambiguous submission before retrying; verify callbacks and use idempotent settlement. Keep application-owned job state, cancellation policy and business approvals. Admit server-side tool execution or agent recursion only with separately proven bounds and explicit delegation.

Consequences and tradeoffs

Durable orchestration and reconciliation add implementation cost. Some workloads remain native/provider-specific rather than fully normalized. Separate pools can protect interactive inference but introduce more deployment and quota allocation work.

Required validation

Crash at upload, submission and completion; repeat notifications; cancel late; rotate credentials and lose a region. Verify no unauthorized resource access, unbounded attempts, hidden charges or duplicate business actions.

Context

Routing, translation, prompt edits and semantic caching can alter results even when infrastructure is healthy. A gateway cannot establish that an answer is correct for the business or that retrieved documents are authorized for the current user. Quality and safety are application-specific contracts.

Options considered

  • Use transport success as quality acceptance.
  • Maintain versioned task, retrieval and policy evaluations.
  • Delegate all quality judgment to the provider or gateway vendor.

Proposed decision

Assign each application an owner for a representative evaluation corpus, output schema, retrieval permissions, tool behavior and acceptable error classes. Context

  • Run controlled and live comparative tests with full policy enabled.

Use a controlled upstream to measure gateway overhead and failure behavior, then approved live providers for semantic and end-to-end timing. AR-ADR-005Use distinct accountable workload identitiesProposed
AreaArchitecture and trustSuggested ownerIdentity platformDrafted8 October 2026

Context

Sharing a gateway or provider credential across unrelated applications prevents reliable revocation and attribution. Routing headers and model names are not authenticators; a provider key proves backend authority, not the identity of the original caller.

Options considered

  • One shared gateway token
  • Application-supplied tenant metadata
  • Verified per-workload identities with accountable owners

Proposed decision

Give each application/environment a distinct authenticated identity and an owner. Derive tenant and cost descriptors from that identity through controlled mapping. Keep administrative credentials out of runtime clients. Define expiry, rotation, decommissioning and emergency revocation, and use separate break-glass administration with auditing.

Consequences and tradeoffs

Attribution and containment improve, but the organization must operate an identity lifecycle and mapping service. Identity outages now require a deliberate service failure policy rather than implicit anonymous operation.

AR-ADR-006Separate caller validation from backend delegationProposed
AreaArchitecture and trustSuggested ownerSecurity architectDrafted8 October 2026

Context

A correctly signed token may have the wrong issuer or audience. A delegated credential may be absent, malformed or intended for another backend; fallback to a configured shared key can silently change who authorizes the action.

Options considered

  • Forward incoming credentials generically
  • Allow shared-key fallback everywhere
  • Validate each authority and forbid implicit delegation fallback

Proposed decision

Validate issuer, audience, lifetime and required claims at the caller boundary. Forward only specifically approved backend credentials, preferably through trusted metadata, and deny missing delegated authority on delegation-required routes. Configure metadata forwarding deliberately. Treat MCP issuer and session identity rules as part of the same reviewed authority model, not as optional decorations.

Consequences and tradeoffs

This prevents convenience fallback from escalating privilege. It requires separate client/provider token lifecycles and can reject requests that previously worked using a shared service account.

Required validation

Use wrong-audience/issuer tokens, duplicate headers, missing metadata and partial credentials. Record the credential fingerprint observed by a controlled backend. Verify unverified claims never influence policy.

Acceptance gates: AR-T03 · AR-T05 · AR-T14. Status: not executed.

Revisit trigger

Identity configuration change, new provider delegation method or token-exchange feature adoption.

  • Disable all retries
  • One declared owner with bounded recoverable attempts

Proposed decision

Choose one retry owner for inference and propagate a total deadline. Classify failures before retry, cap attempts and re-check each destination’s authority. Some failures reach callers earlier, but duplicate execution and hidden cost are controlled. Integrations must disable or account for lower-level retries rather than relying on unrelated defaults.

Select and pin one tracing convention, disable message-content capture by default, and allow only approved low-cardinality identity/model attributes.
